title: Tvashtr cursed Indra. The curse killed his own son.
angle: A father brews a monster to kill the god who murdered his son. He says one sentence over it. That sentence kills the monster instead. Kicker: The Sanskrit explains why the curse backfired: 'indraśatru' with the accent in one place means 'Indra's killer', in another 'whose killer is Indra'. Tvashtr got the accent wrong. In the Veda, even a curse has to be pronounced correctly.
notes:
Arc: Tvashtr's three-headed son Vishvarupa drinks Soma with one mouth, liquor with another; Indra cuts off all three heads (birds fly out of each mouth). Tvashtr excludes Indra from Soma; Indra drinks it uninvited. Tvashtr pours the leftover on the fire with the words 'Grow, having Indra as your foe' (indraśatru), and it rolls out as Vritra, growing an arrow's range a day. Indra wins over Agni and Soma from inside Vritra, strikes, and Vritra collapses 'like a leather bottle drained'. Vritra asks to be cut in two: one half becomes the moon, the other the bellies of living beings.

Playbook: Indra series, episode: the trickster who out-drank his enemy. The accent point lives in the Sanskrit (meaning field), not in Eggeling's English ('Grow thou, having Indra for thy foe!'); phrase the kicker as the text does, or add the grammarians' explanation as a producer note so the fact-checker allows it. F9 watch: 'why birds from the mouths?' is answered in the text (partridge, sparrow, francolin), so say it.

Hindi hook draft: त्वष्टा ने अपने बेटे के हत्यारे को मारने के लिए एक राक्षस बनाया। उस पर एक वाक्य बोला। उसी वाक्य ने राक्षस को मार दिया।

title: Indra made a clone of himself. His wife could not tell them apart.
angle: Indra built a charioteer out of his own thigh, in his own image. The first person fooled was his wife. Kicker: Every charioteer's turban and the dust on his shoulders, says the text, come from a husband trying to tell himself apart from his double. The joke of the Jaiminiya is that even Indra could not keep his own identity.
notes:
Arc: Kutsa Aurava, fashioned from Indra's thighs, looks exactly like him; Indra makes him charioteer. Shachi Paulomi embraces Kutsa by mistake: 'I could not tell you two apart.' Indra shaves Kutsa bald; Kutsa sleeps under a turban. Indra pours dust between his shoulders; Kutsa covers it. She embraces him again. Indra throws him out as a cheat; Kutsa begs 'give us something to live by, we were born from you', shakes off the dust, and a whole people (the Rajas) rise from it, with kings and a priest, Upagu Sausravasa, who bans sacrifice. Indra comes to Upagu three times, 'let me sacrifice for you', and three times the people defeat him for it.

Playbook: Indra series: Indra the insecure husband. Pure comedy with a sting; keep the three disguises as the rhythm (refrain of doubt, guide §2). The Upagu tail (3.200-3.201) can be cut at 'a people rose from the dust'. Companion micro: JB 1.227 (Kutsa and Lusha both call Indra; Lusha ties him by the testicles with a hundred straps; Indra splits himself between them) is too bawdy for the channel but worth a pinned-comment tease.

Hindi hook draft: इंद्र ने अपनी जांघ से अपना हमशक्ल बनाया, सारथी के तौर पर। सबसे पहले धोखा उनकी पत्नी शची ने खाया।

title: A queen in mourning. An old man who would not stop dancing.
angle: The king's army had lost; the queen's brother was dead. An old beggar with a pole on his shoulder danced beside her, smearing her with ghee, and would not go away. Kicker: Indra did not arrive with a thunderbolt. He arrived as the man you shove away. The Jaiminiya says the god comes to the house that is grieving, and comes in disguise.
notes:
Arc: Upama Savedasi, wife of King Pratardana, runs about lamenting her brother. Indra sees her, puts on a dry hide, hangs a cake on one end of a carrying-pole and clotted milk on the other, and dances near her all day, smearing ghee on her whenever she pushes him off. At night her husband asks what she saw; from her description he knows: 'Indra has come to our invocation. Don't harm him. Make him your ally.' Next day the old man dances further off; she chases him and they trade riddling insults ('may your pole break' / 'even broken, the father will mend it'). He runs to her: 'Let us win the battle!', shakes the hairs from the deer-hide, horse-chariots rise from them, and the battle is won.

Playbook: Indra series + a woman lead. The riddle exchange is partly untranslatable (mahira, pevasma); use two or three clear lines and let the rest be dance. The 'Bharadvaja said we did not run to a wife' tag is ritual etymology, drop it.

Hindi hook draft: रानी का भाई मारा गया था। एक बूढ़ा, कंधे पर बहंगी, उसके पास नाचता रहा, घी पोतता रहा, हटाओ तो फिर पास आ जाता।

title: Indra swore not to kill him by day or night, wet or dry. So he used foam at dusk.
angle: Indra had given a demon his word: not by day, not by night, not with anything wet, not with anything dry. Then the demon stole his strength with liquor. Kicker: The Rigveda already sings 'with foam of water, Indra, you tore off Namuci's head'. Indra did not break his word. He found the one hour and the one substance the word did not cover. In the Veda, cleverness is not cheating.
notes:
Arc: Namuci the Asura, with sura liquor, carries off Indra's strength, the essence of food, the Soma. Indra runs to the Ashvins and Sarasvati: 'I have sworn to Namuci, I will slay you neither by day nor by night, neither with staff nor with bow, neither with the flat nor the fist, neither dry nor wet; and he has taken these from me. Bring them back.' They ask for a share, then pour out foam of water as a thunderbolt: 'it is neither dry nor wet', and at the junction of night and day, 'neither day nor night', Indra strikes off Namuci's head with it.

Playbook: Indra series: the lawyer-god. F9: viewers will ask 'is a loophole honest?'; the kicker should take a side (F11). The Rigveda verse 8.14.13 is quoted inside SB 12.7.3.4 so it can be cited from the packet. The Mahabharata retells it for Vritra (see epic tier).

Hindi hook draft: इंद्र ने नमुचि को वचन दिया था: ना दिन में मारूंगा, ना रात में, ना सूखे से, ना गीले से। फिर नमुचि ने शराब पिलाकर उनका बल चुरा लिया।

title: Indra confessed to murder, then said: not a hair of me is harmed.
angle: A king died fighting and came to Indra's house. Indra offered him a boon. The king said: you choose for me. And Indra began to confess. Kicker: The oldest text to list Indra's crimes puts them in Indra's own mouth, as the opening of a lesson on consciousness. The Veda does not hide what the god did. It asks what, in you, is untouched by what you did.
notes:
Arc: Pratardana, son of Divodasa, reaches Indra's abode by valour. 'Choose a boon.' 'Choose it for me.' Indra: 'Know me. That is the most beneficial thing for man. I killed the three-headed son of Tvashtr; I threw the ascetics to the hyenas; I broke many treaties; I killed the Prahladas in the sky, the Paulomas in the air, the Kalakanjas on earth; and not a hair of me was harmed. He who knows me, no deed of his destroys his world, not even killing his mother or father, not theft, not killing an embryo. The colour does not leave his face.' Then: 'I am the breath, the conscious self; worship me as life.' The Aitareya adds the other side: the gods themselves once excluded Indra from Soma for these same crimes.

Playbook: Indra series + F11 argument hybrid (the kind of short that gets comments). Devotional sensitivity: 'killing his mother' is in the text as the extreme case of the knower's immunity, not a licence; frame it as the text's own shock. Pair the AB line (gods list Indra's crimes) as the 'other side'.

Hindi hook draft: राजा प्रतर्दन लड़ते-लड़ते मरकर इंद्र के घर पहुंचे। इंद्र ने वरदान मांगने को कहा। राजा बोले, आप ही चुन लीजिए। और इंद्र ने अपने अपराध गिनाने शुरू किए।

title: Indra asked to become Prajapati. So Prajapati became 'Who'.
angle: After killing Vritra, Indra had one wish left: let me be what you are. The creator asked him back: then who am I? Kicker: The Rigveda's famous refrain 'to which god shall we offer?' (kasmai devaya) has an answer in the Brahmana: to Who. The god with no name got it from Indra's ambition.
notes:
Arc: Indra, about to kill Vritra, asks the gods to back him; when they rush in, he thinks they are coming for him and breathes fire at them; they flee. He kills Vritra alone. Winner of everything, he goes to Prajapati: 'Let me be what you are. Let me be great.' Prajapati: 'Then who am I?' Indra: 'Exactly what you just said.' From then Prajapati's name is Ka, 'Who'; and Indra became great, hence Mahendra.

Playbook: Indra series micro (60-75 s). Needs a visual for 'Who' (an empty throne, an unlabelled altar). Doctrine risk: it is wordplay, keep it as a joke with a kicker.

title: Indra killed Vritra and ran away. He thought he had lost.
angle: The most famous victory in the Veda ended with the winner hiding. Indra threw the bolt, thought he was the weaker, and fled; the gods hid too. Kicker: The hero of the Vedas did not know he had won. Somebody else had to go and look.
notes:
Arc: No one knows if Vritra is dead. The gods send Vayu to check, for the price of the first Soma offering. Vritra is dead, but his stench is unbearable; Vayu blows through him for a second share; the gods push the rest of the smell into cattle and dead bodies. Indra comes out of hiding.

Playbook: Indra series, minor: good as a cold open or a kicker for another Vritra episode; thin as a full short (ritual explanation of the Soma cups). Keith's Taittiriya version (TS 2.5.1, English) is longer and adds that Vritra was swallowing Indra.

title: He taught with a horse's head because teaching with his own meant losing it.
angle: Indra told the sage: teach this secret to anyone and I cut off your head. Two gods still wanted the secret. They found a way that cost the sage his head, twice. Kicker: The Mahabharata's Dadhichi gives his bones for Indra's thunderbolt. The Veda's Dadhyanc gives his head to keep a promise to Indra and a promise to the Ashvins at the same time. Loyalty in the Veda is a logic puzzle solved with a horse.
notes:
Arc: Dadhyanc Atharvana knows the 'honey' doctrine: how the head of the sacrifice is put back on. Indra forbids him on pain of beheading. The Ashvins come as pupils; he tells them of the threat; they say 'we will protect you: we will cut off your head, keep it aside, fix a horse's head on you; you teach us with that; when Indra strikes it off, we put your own head back.' So it happens: the horse-headed sage teaches; Indra cuts off the horse's head; the Ashvins restore his own. The Rigveda remembers it ('Dadhyanc with a horse's head spoke to you the sweet doctrine'), and the Brhaddevata says the horse's head fell into a lake on Mount Sharyanavat, and still rises from the water to grant boons.

Playbook: Indra series + animal + loyalty (F4). SB 14.1.1.24 ends mid-sentence in the corpus (flagged truncated); the RV verse and BD fill it. Devotional tie-in: the horse-headed teacher later becomes Hayagriva.

Hindi hook draft: इंद्र ने ऋषि दध्यंच से कहा: ये रहस्य किसी को सिखाया तो सिर काट दूंगा। अश्विनों को वही रहस्य चाहिए था। रास्ता निकला, जिसमें ऋषि का सिर दो बार कटा।

title: The gods needed someone to carry Indra's sin. They picked the man in the well.
angle: Indra killed a priest's son. Indra is a god, so the sin could not stick to him. It had to go somewhere. Kicker: The Veda keeps both Tritas: the scapegoat who carries a god's guilt, and the man who, from the bottom of a well, demanded that the gods show up. Sometimes they are the same person.
notes:
Arc: Trita, Dvita and Ekata (the Aptyas) follow Indra 'as a Brahman follows a king'. When Indra kills Vishvarupa, the Aptyas 'knew of it', so the guilt passes to them; they pass it on to whoever sacrifices without a fee; the gods make it the rule for the new-moon cake. In the Rigveda and the Brhaddevata, Trita is also the man thrown into a well by 'the sons of the she-wolf' who stole his cows; from the bottom of the well he presses Soma, calls all the gods and reproaches them: 'where is your all-seeing power?' They come, share his offering, and pull him out.

Playbook: Indra series, the uncomfortable one. Two texts, one character; the SB passage is short and ritual, so let the RV well-hymn carry the images (the moon running in the waters, the stars that shine by night and go nowhere by day). F9: say plainly the text says the Aptyas were punished for knowing.

title: The Soma was stolen by a bird. An archer shot one feather off.
angle: Before Indra could drink Soma, somebody had to steal it from heaven. The thief was a falcon. The guard was an archer who never missed. He missed, by a feather. Kicker: The Vedic heist has no hero who stays behind to cover the escape. It has one feather on the ground, and a tree grows from it. Every leaf-plate at a Hindu meal is, the Brahmana says, that feather.
notes:
Arc: A voice declares 'I was Manu, I was Surya' (Vamadeva speaking as Indra), then praises the Bird 'above all birds': the falcon that seized the Soma stalk from the iron fortresses of heaven and flew 'swift as thought', bearing a thousand libations. In 4.27 the seer says 'while in the womb I knew all the births of the gods; a hundred iron fortresses held me; I flew out as a falcon.' The guardian archer Krishanu shoots as the bird speeds down; the Aitareya says the arrow cut off the nail of her left foot (it became a porcupine) and a feather fell (it became the parna tree).

Playbook: Animal protagonist (F4). Mix: RV gives the flight and the archer, AB 13.2 gives the feather/nail aftermath (AB calls the bird Gayatri). 4.27.1 ('I knew all the births while in the womb') is a second story in itself; keep it as one line or drop. Vamadeva is the seer of the published 'Indra's childhood' (4.18): same voice, so a natural series link.

Hindi hook draft: इंद्र सोम पी सकें, उससे पहले किसी को उसे स्वर्ग से चुराना था। चोर एक बाज़ था। पहरेदार एक तीरंदाज़, जो कभी नहीं चूकता था। वो चूका, एक पंख से।

title: Indra's wife versus a monkey: the rudest hymn in the Rigveda.
angle: People have stopped pouring Soma for Indra, because a monkey is eating the offerings. Indra's wife wants it dead. Indra loves the monkey. Kicker: The hymn chanted at the biggest royal sacrifice is a marital spat about a monkey. The priests kept it because, they said, it was Indra's.
notes:
Arc: A three-way dialogue: Indrani complains the ape Vrishakapi has spoiled her things and has grown bold; Indra defends his pet; the ape answers; the quarrel turns bawdy (Indrani's boast of her own charms, Indra's 'my wife is the best of women'), ends with the ape's return and a feast (the dog, the boar, the tame beast slaughtered), and the refrain 'Indra is above all'. Brhaddevata reads the ape as the sun.

Playbook: Hold for a mature-audience test; several verses are explicit in Griffith's Latin and in any honest Hindi. Funny, famous among scholars, risky with devotees. If made: play it as a domestic comedy with the ape as the third character, never a lecture about 'what it really means'.

title: The first woman to win a chariot race did it with one bull and a wooden club.
angle: Everyone else had horses. Mudgala had one bull, a club for the other side of the yoke, and a wife who could drive. Kicker: The Rigveda's only named woman charioteer did not ask to be included in the race. She drove, and the hymn says the dust of her bull's hooves was the shout of victory.
notes:
Arc: Mudgala's cattle are stolen (or he is poor); he yokes a lone bull with a wooden club, and Mudgalani takes the reins ('the wife of Mudgala drove'). The bull runs mad, 'his dung flies', the club does its work; Indra speeds the car; they win the thousand and recover the cows. The Brhaddevata says with this hymn Mudgala overcame Indra and Soma in a contest, yoking a bull and a mallet to his chariot.

Playbook: Woman lead; animal; Indra as helper, so an Indra-series side-episode. Griffith's text of 10.102 is obscure in places; the writer should keep to the clear verses (1, 2, 5-9) and let the pictures run. F3: open on the bull and the club, name Mudgalani by 5 s.

Hindi hook draft: बाकी सबके पास घोड़े थे। मुद्गल के पास एक बैल था, जुए के दूसरी तरफ़ एक लकड़ी का मूसल, और एक पत्नी जो रथ चला सकती थी।

title: Indra was jealous of his own gang. A sage had to talk him down.
angle: Agastya cooked an offering for Indra, then gave it to the Maruts. Indra arrived to find his food gone and his army fed. Kicker: The god who could not share the credit learned to share the cup. The Rigveda's hymn of reconciliation was written by the mediator, not the winner.
notes:
Arc: The Maruts ask Indra why he goes alone; Indra boasts he killed Vritra alone, 'where were you?'; the Maruts remind him of their help; he relents ('I feared nothing when you were with me'). In 1.170 the tone turns: 'Why, brother, do you want to kill us?' The Brhaddevata frames it: Agastya prepared an oblation for Indra and praised the Maruts; Indra, reading his intent, confronted him; Agastya pacified him, and from then the Maruts drink Soma with Indra.

Playbook: Indra series: Indra the insecure leader. Dialogue hymn, so the voice can switch characters. Agastya is the husband of the published Lopamudra short: same seer, new story.

title: Indra's daughter-in-law complained he skipped her feast. He turned up with riddles.
angle: 'All my other friends are here. Only my father-in-law has not come.' The father-in-law is Indra. Kicker: Even Indra had in-laws. And he answered a complaint with a riddle contest, which is how the Veda says a family makes peace.
notes:
Arc: Vasukra's wife, Indra's daughter-in-law, laments that Indra has not come to the Soma; Indra arrives ('I am the one for whom the bull was cooked') and the hymn turns into riddles: the hare swallowing the razor, the fox stealing up on the lion, the jackal hunting the boar. Brhaddevata: the Bolt-bearer, hearing her, came that moment and stood on the northern altar.

Playbook: Minor; the riddles are hard to picture. Good as a pinned-comment story or a 45-second filler in the series.

title: Indra went into hiding, and a human was made king of the gods. He wanted Indra's wife.
angle: After killing Vritra, Indra hid inside a lotus stalk. Heaven needed a king, so the gods crowned a man. The man's first demand was Indra's wife. Kicker: The Mahabharata makes Indra's greatest enemy not a demon but the man who replaced him. Nahusha was undone by one word to a sage, the word that became his new body.
notes:
Arc: Indra, guilt-struck after Vritra, vanishes; Nahusha is made king of the gods and asks for Shachi. She stalls: 'come to me in a palanquin carried by sages.' Nahusha has the seven seers carry him and kicks Agastya, 'sarpa, sarpa' (move!); Agastya's curse turns him into a serpent (sarpa). Shachi finds Indra with Brhaspati's help; he returns after expiation.

Playbook: Epic tier (Mahabharata, Ganguli sections 5.11-5.17: Udyoga Parva). Confirm the exact section span where Nahusha's fall and 'sarpa' pun sit before scripting; Ganguli chapters are long, so the packet will be big. Devotional sensitivity: Indra as a guilty, hiding god is the text's own portrait; audience comments ask exactly for this.

Hindi hook draft: वृत्र को मारकर इंद्र कमल की डंडी में छिप गए। स्वर्ग को राजा चाहिए था, तो देवताओं ने एक इंसान को ताज पहनाया। इंसान की पहली मांग थी इंद्र की पत्नी।

title: Indra went looking for the demon king he had beaten. He found him living as a donkey.
angle: Indra could not find Bali anywhere in the three worlds. Brahma told him: look in an empty house, in the body of a donkey. Kicker: The winner came to gloat and left with a lecture on losing. The Mahabharata lets the demon have the last word, and lets Indra listen.
notes:
Arc: Indra, curious how the mighty Bali lives after his fall, finds him as an ass in an empty house and taunts him. Bali answers with the longest, calmest speech on Time in the Mahabharata: 'you did not win, Time won; I grieve not; what you own will pass from you too.' Shri (Fortune) then leaves Bali and comes to Indra, and tells Indra why she stays with no one.

Playbook: Epic tier (Shanti Parva). Indra series: Indra the student again, which is the trait the audience named (F7). Keep the Shri sequel as the kicker or a part 2; the Bali speech must be cut hard to three images.

title: Indra became a student to learn why Prahlada could not be defeated. Then he asked for it as his fee.
angle: Prahlada ruled the three worlds and could not be beaten in battle. Indra went to him disguised as a Brahmin student and asked one question: what makes you unbeatable? Kicker: Indra did not win with a weapon. He won by asking a good man to give away the one thing that made him good, and the good man kept his word. The Mahabharata does not say who is the villain here.
notes:
Arc: Prahlada, the demon king, is undefeatable through 'shila', good conduct. Indra serves him as a student for years; when Prahlada offers a boon, Indra asks for his shila. Bound by his word, Prahlada gives it; a shining form leaves his body (Conduct), then Dharma follows it, then Truth, then Good Deeds, then Strength, then Shri herself: 'where conduct goes, I go.' Prahlada asks who the student was; she tells him: Indra.

Playbook: Epic tier (Shanti Parva, one long Ganguli section). Indra series, dark episode; F10 (emotion → shares): injustice. F6 trap: do not open on 'you think Prahlada's story is about Narasimha'; open on the disguised student.

title: Indra came begging in a Brahmin's robe. Karna cut his own skin off to pay him.
angle: Karna was born with armour grown into his skin. Indra wanted it off him before the war. He came at noon, when Karna refuses no one. Kicker: Indra's cheating gave Arjuna the war. Karna's keeping his word cost him everything, and he knew it in advance. The epic says the god blushed.
notes:
Arc: Surya warns Karna in a dream that Indra will come disguised to beg the armour and earrings; Karna refuses to refuse. Indra comes; Karna cuts the armour from his body, blood running, and hands it over; Indra, ashamed, gives him the single-use spear. The gods shout; Karna is called Vaikartana, the cutter.

Playbook: Epic tier, very well known; the value is the Indra angle for the series (the god who begs). Companion: Indra as hawk testing Shibi (animal section).

title: A hawk demanded the pigeon back. The king gave his own flesh instead.
angle: A pigeon flew into King Shibi's lap, chased by a hawk. The hawk spoke: that is my food. Give it back. The king said: take me instead. Kicker: The gods did not test whether the king was generous. They tested whether he would keep protecting someone after it stopped being cheap.
notes:
Arc: Shibi refuses to surrender the refugee bird; the hawk argues like a lawyer (the hunter must eat too; you deprive my chicks); the king offers a bull, then his own flesh, equal to the pigeon's weight. He cuts and cuts; the scale will not balance; he climbs onto it himself. The hawk is Indra, the pigeon Agni; they reveal themselves and restore him.

Playbook: Epic tier (Vana Parva). Animal + loyalty (F4) + Indra series crossover. One of the most shareable stories in the corpus (emotion → shares, F10).

Hindi hook draft: एक कबूतर राजा शिबि की गोद में आ गिरा, पीछे एक बाज़। बाज़ ने कहा: वो मेरा खाना है, लौटा दो। राजा ने कहा: मुझे ले लो।

title: The thunderbolt was a dead sage's spine.
angle: No weapon could kill Vritra. The gods went to a living sage and asked for his bones. Kicker: In the Veda Dadhyanc lost his head to keep a secret. In the epic he gives his whole skeleton to end a war. The same name, a thousand years apart, and the thing he gives up grows.
notes:
Arc: Vishnu tells the gods only a weapon made from Dadhicha's bones can kill Vritra; the sage gives up his body; Tvashtr makes the vajra; Indra kills Vritra; the demons flee into the sea and plot by night to kill the sages. (The Vedic root is the Ashvins' Dadhyanc, see the horse-head story.)

Playbook: Epic tier; companion to indra-dadhyanc-horse-head. Risk: 'everyone knows this'; the hook must start on the sage, not on Vritra.

title: Indra's punishment, and the ram that gave him back his manhood.
angle: Everyone knows Ahalya became a stone. Few know what Gautama did to Indra, and what the gods used to repair him. Kicker: The Valmiki Ramayana says Ahalya was not fooled. And Indra's excuse to the gods was: I did it for you. The oldest telling is uglier and more honest than the stone.
notes:
Arc: Indra, in Gautama's shape, seduces Ahalya, who knows him and consents; Gautama returns, curses Indra to lose his testicles and Ahalya to live unseen on ashes for a thousand years until Rama comes. Indra, 'deprived of my scrotum', complains to the gods that he did it to serve them (to break Gautama's ascetic power); the gods fit him with a ram's testicles, taken from the ram of the sacrifice. Rama arrives; Ahalya is restored.

Playbook: Epic tier (Bala Kanda, Dutt). Indra series, the fall. Adult content; devotional sensitivity high (Ahalya's consent is in the text, 1.47). F6 trap: do not open on 'you think she was a stone'. Open on Gautama's door.

title: The day Indra lost to a cowherd, and crowned him anyway.
angle: Krishna told the cowherds to stop worshipping Indra. Indra answered with seven days of rain. Kicker: In the Harivamsa Indra does not sulk. He comes down, admits it, and gives the boy a new name. The audience that wants Indra redeemed should see the one story where he redeems himself.
notes:
Arc: Krishna argues that cowherds should worship the mountain and the cows, not the rain-god; the Govardhana festival is held; Indra, insulted, sends the clouds of doom; Krishna lifts the mountain as an umbrella for seven days; Indra comes down, accepts, and anoints Krishna 'Govinda', lord of cows, with milk from Surabhi.

Playbook: Epic tier (Harivamsa, Dutt translation; the corpus has it in English). Indra series, closing episode candidate. The published channel has a Samaveda-Krishna short; this is a different cut.

title: Indra was taken prisoner by a teenager.
angle: Ravana's son fought the king of the gods, tied him up, and carried him to Lanka. Brahma had to come and negotiate the ransom. Kicker: The god who was 'never harmed' ended up a hostage in a demon's palace, and the Ramayana says he deserved it.
notes:
Arc: Meghanada fights Indra, uses invisibility, binds him and takes him to Lanka; Brahma comes to Ravana's court to bargain; Meghanada asks for immortality, gets a conditional boon instead, and the title Indrajit; Indra is released. Brahma reminds Indra it is the price of Ahalya (in the Uttara Kanda's version).

Playbook: Epic tier (Uttara Kanda). Dutt's Uttara Kanda sections 7.32 (the march on Indra's heaven) to 7.35 (Brahma names him Indrajit and recalls Ahalya); numbering differs from the critical edition.

title: She grew old in her father's house, sick and unmarried. Then she wrote to the twin gods.
angle: Ghosha stayed in her father's house past the age of marriage, with a disease on her skin. Her father was a famous poet. She wrote her own hymn. Kicker: The Rigveda has two hymns by a woman who refused to be a story told about her. She listed the gods' record like a lawyer and asked for her turn. The published Apala made a deal with Indra; Ghosha filed a claim with the Ashvins.
notes:
Arc: Ghosha, daughter of Kakshivat, calls the Ashvins' chariot 'as easy to invoke as a father's name', lists every rescue they ever did (Bhujyu from the sea, Rebha from the well, the old Chyavana made young, the mare's foal, the bride for Vimada), and asks them: you did all that for strangers, do it for me. 10.40 is her wedding-eve hymn ('the bride goes to the groom's house'). The Brhaddevata records that the Nasatyas gave Ghosha a husband.

Playbook: Woman lead; direct successor to Apala (the hit). F3: open on the skin and the father's house. The Ashvin catalogue in 10.39 is where the Bhujyu, Rebha, Vandana stories can be dropped as one-line images.

Hindi hook draft: घोषा पिता के घर में बूढ़ी होती रही, बीमार, अविवाहित। पिता मशहूर कवि थे। उसने अपना सूक्त खुद लिखा।

title: He offered her half of everything. She asked whether it would make her immortal.
angle: The richest sage in Videha was leaving home. He called his wife to divide the property. She asked a question that made him sit back down. Kicker: The second wife, the text says, 'knew only what women know'. The first wife refused the money. Only one of them has an Upanishad named after her conversation.
notes:
Arc: Yajnavalkya: 'I am going away; let me settle between you and Katyayani.' Maitreyi: 'If this whole earth full of wealth were mine, would I be immortal by it?' 'No. Your life would be like the life of the rich.' 'Then what would I do with what does not make me immortal? Tell me what you know.' He teaches: the husband is dear not for the husband's sake but for the self's; the lump of salt dissolved in water; 'after death there is no consciousness, that is what I say'. She: 'you have confused me.' He explains: where there is duality one sees another; where all is self, who sees whom?

Playbook: Woman lead, philosophy (saves, F10). Madhavananda's translation in the corpus interleaves Shankara's commentary; the writer must use only the dialogue lines. The 'other wife knew only what women know' line is the text's, and it is the hook's edge; do not soften, do not lecture.

Hindi hook draft: विदेह के सबसे धनी ऋषि याज्ञवल्क्य घर छोड़ने चले। पत्नी मैत्रेयी को बुलाया, संपत्ति बांटने। उसने एक सवाल पूछा, और ऋषि वापस बैठ गए।

title: A woman stood up in the king's assembly with two questions, like an archer with two arrows.
angle: King Janaka put a thousand cows in a pen for the wisest man present. Yajnavalkya told his pupil to drive them home before the debate began. Then a woman stood up. Kicker: Two people were warned that day that a question could cost them their head. The woman knew when to stop. The man did not. The Upanishad lets her declare the winner.
notes:
Arc: Gargi Vachaknavi asks what water is woven on, then air, then the sky, upward until Yajnavalkya says 'do not ask too much, Gargi, or your head will fall off.' She stops. Later she rises again: 'like a warrior from Kashi with two arrows'; she asks about what is above heaven, below earth, between; he answers 'the imperishable', in which space is woven. She tells the Brahmins: 'bow to him; none of you will defeat him.' Then Shakalya keeps pushing, 'how many gods?', three hundred and three, thirty-three, six, three, two, one and a half, one; Yajnavalkya warns him; he asks once more, and his head falls off, and robbers carry away his bones thinking they are something else.

Playbook: Woman lead + death stakes. BU 3.9 is long; cite 3.9.1-3.9.26 but script only the countdown of gods and the head. SB 11.6.3 and JB 2.75-2.77 have the cows episode in English too. Expect comments about 'head will fall off' (the text's idiom for a debate forfeit; say so in one line, F9).

Hindi hook draft: जनक ने हज़ार गायें बांध दीं, सबसे ज्ञानी के लिए। याज्ञवल्क्य ने शिष्य से कहा, बहस से पहले ही हांक ले जाओ। फिर एक स्त्री खड़ी हुई।

title: A queen's spell to rule her husband and crush her rivals. It is in the Rigveda.
angle: 'My sons kill their enemies. My daughter is a queen. I have conquered my husband.' The woman speaking is Indra's wife. Kicker: The Veda's model of a wife is not a silent one. It is a woman at dawn announcing that she has won. Six verses, no apology.
notes:
Arc: Shachi Paulomi (per the tradition) speaks in the first person as the sun rises: 'I am the banner and the head; my husband obeys my will; I have seized the glory of the other wives; I am victorious over my rivals, that I may hold imperial sway over this hero and his people.'

Playbook: Woman's first-person voice; Indra crossover. No plot, so build the arc around a palace morning (the co-wives, the rising sun, the sons). Companion: 10.145, the herb spell against a rival wife (same genre, anonymous speaker) can supply the images of the rival being 'blown away like a leaf'.

title: She dug a plant at dawn and whispered her rival's name into it. Then she did not say the name.
angle: A woman digs up a herb to drive away her husband's other wife: 'Her very name I utter not.' Kicker: The Rigveda preserved a co-wife's spell word for word, and its sharpest line is the thing she refused to say.
notes:
Arc: The speaker digs 'the most effectual plant', blows the rival away, claims to be stronger, refuses to speak her name, and binds the husband 'as a cow hastens to her calf'.

Playbook: Micro; pair with shachi-co-wife-spell rather than run alone. Risk: no protagonist with a name.

title: The gods sold a goddess to buy Soma. Then they stole her back with a song.
angle: Soma was in heaven; the gods were on earth. The Gandharvas who guarded it loved women. The gods had one woman: Speech. Kicker: Faced with scholars and musicians, the goddess of language chose the musicians. The Brahmana says that is why women to this day prefer the one who sings. The Veda invented the vina to win back a woman.
notes:
Arc: Gayatri as a bird steals Soma; the Gandharva Vishvavasu snatches it. 'Gandharvas are fond of women; send Vac; she will come back.' They trade: Soma for Vac, 'as long as she wishes to stay'. The Gandharvas recite the Vedas to her: 'see how we know!' The gods invent the lute and sit playing and singing: 'thus we will amuse you.' She turns to the gods. In the Aitareya, Speech herself proposes the bargain, and the gods first refuse: 'how could we be without you?'

Playbook: Music angle (F8: the audience notices and talks about music). F6 trap: not 'Soma was really a drink'; open on the sale. The text's 'women are fond of the one who sings' line is the kicker, say it as the text's claim.

Hindi hook draft: सोम स्वर्ग में था, देवता धरती पर। सोम के पहरेदार गंधर्व स्त्रियों के शौकीन थे। देवताओं के पास एक ही स्त्री थी: वाक्, यानी वाणी।

title: Fortune was born shining, and the gods' first thought was to rob her.
angle: Shri came out of Prajapati resplendent and trembling. The gods looked at her and said: let us kill her and take all this. Kicker: The goddess of wealth was not given wealth. She was stripped of it, told to earn it back, and did, item by item, from the gods who took it. That is the Veda's origin of Lakshmi.
notes:
Arc: Prajapati forbids the killing ('she is a woman; one does not kill women') but lets them take: Agni takes her food, Soma her royal power, Varuna her sovereignty, Mitra her rank, Indra her strength, Brhaspati her holy lustre, Savitr her dominion, Pushan her wealth, Sarasvati her prosperity, Tvashtr her beauty. She complains; Prajapati: 'ask it back by sacrifice.' She invents the ten-dish offering and, naming each god, takes back each thing.

Playbook: Devotional sensitivity: gods robbing Lakshmi; it is the text's own story and ends with her winning. Keep the list of ten to four or five images (food, power, strength, beauty).

title: Mind and Speech argued over who was greater. Speech lost, and stopped speaking.
angle: 'I say what you only think.' 'You only say what I have already thought.' They went to Prajapati to decide. Kicker: Because Speech once lost an argument, one god in the Veda is still worshipped without a word.
notes:
Arc: Mind: 'you only speak what I understand'; Speech: 'what you know, I make known'. Prajapati rules for Mind ('speech imitates you'). Speech, gainsaid, is dismayed and miscarries; she refuses to carry oblations for Prajapati, so he is offered to in silence.

Playbook: Micro (45-60 s). Good interstitial for the series on Vac (pair with vac-sold-for-soma).

title: The gods raced for the bride. The twins won on a donkey cart.
angle: Surya, the Sun's daughter, was to be married. The gods decided the groomsmen by a race. Agni was fastest, Ushas was the dawn, Indra had the horses. The Ashvins turned up with asses. Kicker: Every Hindu wedding still recites mantras from Surya's wedding. Few know the groomsmen were chosen by a race, and the slowest animal won.
notes:
Arc: Prajapati gives his daughter Surya Savitri to King Soma; all the gods come as groomsmen; they race for her: Agni on a mule-cart, Ushas on red cows, Indra on horses, the Ashvins on an ass-cart; each bargains for a share as it is overtaken; the Ashvins win the bride, and that is why the Ashvina litany is theirs. The Rigveda wedding hymn (10.85) describes the bride's journey, 'the Ashvins were the wooers'.

Playbook: Explainer risk (F1): keep one protagonist, the Ashvins (underdogs, physicians, excluded from Soma). The AB passage is dense with ritual; use only the race. RV 10.85 verses 6-16 for the wedding pictures.

title: A king who had been turned into a woman, and the wife who prayed him back.
angle: Asanga, son of Playoga, was changed into a woman by a curse. His wife Shashvati composed a verse. The seer Medhatithi changed him back. Kicker: The Rigveda contains a verse by a woman celebrating that her husband is a man again. Three thousand years ago gender was already a story people told.
notes:
Arc: The Brhaddevata records the curse and the restoration in two lines; the Rigveda keeps Shashvati's verse rejoicing at her husband's manhood restored (8.1.34) and Asanga's gift of ten thousand cattle to the singer.

Playbook: Fascinating, thin in the corpus (BD 6.40 text, RV verse explicit). Treat as a pinned-comment or part of a 'strange verses' compilation, not a stand-alone short unless the producer wants the risk.

title: She followed Death into the forest and out-talked him.
angle: She chose a husband who had one year to live. On the day, she walked behind Yama as he carried the soul away, and would not go home. Kicker: The boy Nachiketa won from Death with silence and refusal. Savitri won with argument. Both are in the same tradition, and only one of them is told as a 'wife's duty'.
notes:
Arc: Savitri chooses Satyavan knowing Narada's prophecy; on the day she fasts, accompanies him to the forest; Yama comes in person; she follows him, speaking of dharma until he grants boons: her father-in-law's sight and kingdom, her father's sons, and 'a hundred sons for me', which cannot happen without Satyavan. Yama laughs and returns the soul.

Playbook: Epic tier (Vana Parva). Woman lead; natural pairing with the queued Nachiketa short (same opponent). The 'devoted wife' frame is the trap (F6): open on her walking behind Yama.

Hindi hook draft: सावित्री ने वो पति चुना जिसके पास एक साल था। उस दिन, यम उसकी आत्मा ले चले, और सावित्री पीछे-पीछे चलती रही, लौटी नहीं।

title: The king denied knowing her. She answered him in front of his whole court.
angle: Shakuntala walked into Dushyanta's hall with their son. The king said: I do not know you. There was no ring in this version. Kicker: Kalidasa gave the king a magic excuse. The Mahabharata gave him none. In the older story the only magic is a woman refusing to be told she is lying.
notes:
Arc: In the Mahabharata (not Kalidasa) there is no ring, no curse: the king simply lies. Shakuntala's speech: a wife is half the man; a son is the father reborn; 'you alone know your own truth; the gods who live in the heart see it'; she turns to leave. A voice from the sky confirms the boy; Dushyanta says he feared the court would doubt; the boy is Bharata, after whom the land is named.

Playbook: Epic tier (Adi Parva). F6 trap: 'you think there was a ring' is a correction hook; open instead on the hall and the child. The Bharata naming is the kicker's second beat (and links to AB 39.9, Bharata's horse-sacrifices).

title: A princess threw a Brahmin's daughter into a well. The Brahmin's daughter made her a servant.
angle: Two girls fought over a dress. One was the king's daughter, one the priest's. The priest's daughter ended up in a well, and then on top. Kicker: Of the two women, the one who was made a servant became the mother of the line that leads to the Kurus. The Mahabharata keeps score over centuries.
notes:
Arc: Devayani (daughter of Shukra, priest of the demons) and Sharmishtha (the demon king's daughter) quarrel; Sharmishtha pushes her into a well; Yayati pulls her out by the hand. Devayani demands Sharmishtha as her maid as the price of her father's priesthood; the demon king agrees. Devayani marries Yayati; Sharmishtha, the maid, secretly bears Yayati three sons; Devayani discovers it; Shukra curses Yayati with old age.

Playbook: Epic tier. Women's rivalry story with a sting; leads into yayati-puru. Keep Kacha (the previous chapters) as a separate short.

title: A mother's speech to a son who would not fight. The Mahabharata preserved every word.
angle: Her son had lost his kingdom and lay in bed. Vidula stood over him and said: either blaze for a moment or smoulder for a lifetime. Kicker: Kunti sent this to her sons instead of a blessing. The most ferocious speech in the Mahabharata before the war is a mother's.
notes:
Arc: Kunti tells Krishna the old story to carry to Yudhishthira: Vidula's son Sanjaya, defeated, lies depressed; she rains contempt and argument on him ('I did not bear you to be a eunuch of fortune'); he answers; she wins; he rises and fights.

Playbook: Epic tier (Udyoga Parva). Argument short (F11) with a protagonist. Dark on gender ('eunuch', 'is my womb to blame'); keep the text's own force without adding.

title: A snake killed her son. A fowler caught the snake. She refused to let it die.
angle: The fowler dragged the snake to the mother in a noose: say the word and it dies. The mother said: killing it will not bring my son back. Then the snake spoke. Kicker: A courtroom with four defendants (snake, Death, Time, karma) and a mother who refuses to be the executioner. The Mahabharata opens its last book of teachings not with a sage but with her.
notes:
Arc: Gautami's son dies of snakebite; Arjunaka the fowler brings the snake; she refuses revenge; the snake says 'Death sent me'; Death appears: 'Time sent me'; Time: 'the boy's own deeds sent him'; each defendant hands the blame up the chain, and the boy's karma is the final answer; the fowler frees the snake.

Playbook: Epic tier (Anushasana Parva, one long section). Animal + loyalty to principle + argument (comments) + grief (shares). Strong candidate for the 'argument inside a story' test (F11).

Hindi hook draft: बहेलिया सांप को फंदे में बांधकर मां के पास लाया: कह दो, मार दूं। मां बोली: इसे मारने से मेरा बेटा नहीं लौटेगा। तब सांप बोला।

title: The dogs held a Vedic chant. The subject was lunch.
angle: A student went out to study the Veda. A white dog appeared. The other dogs asked it: revered sir, please sing for us, we are hungry. Kicker: The Upanishad that teaches the secret of Om also records dogs performing a flawless Soma chant for breakfast. It is either the oldest satire of priests, or the oldest admission that hunger is holy. The text does not say which.
notes:
Arc: Baka Dalbhya sees a white dog; small dogs gather and ask it to sing them food; 'come tomorrow morning'. Next morning the dogs move in a line, each holding the tail of the one in front, exactly as priests do holding each other at the chant, sit, say 'Him', and chant: 'Om, let us eat! Om, let us drink! Om, may the god who gives rain bring us food!'

Playbook: Animal (F4, the channel's two dog shorts out-share everything). Comedy with a real arc (request → promise → performance). One cold open, one image system (the tails). F9 watch: 'is it mocking priests?' Answer in the kicker as the text's ambiguity.

Hindi hook draft: एक विद्यार्थी वेद पढ़ने निकला। एक सफ़ेद कुत्ता आया। बाकी कुत्तों ने उससे कहा: श्रीमान, हमारे लिए गाइए, हमें भूख लगी है।

title: The greatest sage in the Rigveda was caught burgling a god's house by a dog.
angle: Vasishtha was starving. At night he crept into Varuna's house for food. The dog woke up. Kicker: The Rigveda's sleep spell was composed by a hungry sage talking his way past a watchdog. The dog is the son of Sarama, the same dog family as the one who found Indra's cows. In this story the dog is the honest one.
notes:
Arc: The Brhaddevata: Vasishtha, after three days without food, enters Varuna's house at night; a dog runs at him barking; he pacifies it with the verses that are now RV 7.55: 'Son of Sarama, tawny one, your teeth gleam like spears; bark at the thief, not at Indra's singers; sleep, mother, sleep, father, sleep dog, sleep master of the house; the women sleeping in the court, we close their eyes as we close this house.' The dog sleeps; the sage goes in.

Playbook: Animal + a sage behaving badly; the Dog and Sarama shorts were the channel's biggest. BD 6.11 and 6.13 are truncated in the corpus; the RV hymn is complete, and the burglary frame is in BD 6.12 which is intact. The 'house of Varuna' and the famine are also in the later Vasishtha tradition; keep to BD.

Hindi hook draft: वसिष्ठ भूखे थे। रात में वरुण के घर में घुसे, कुछ खाने को। कुत्ता जाग गया।

title: The god of fire ran away from his job. A fish told the gods where he was.
angle: Agni had three elder brothers. All three died carrying offerings to the gods. So Agni hid in the water. Kicker: The Veda's first recorded resignation letter was written by Fire, and the first severance package was negotiated by the god everyone thought was the servant. He only came back with a contract.
notes:
Arc: Taittiriya: Agni, afraid of the fate of his brothers, enters the waters; the gods search; a fish betrays him; Agni curses it: 'may they kill you at pleasure, since you told'; the gods promise him the first and last offering and 'life unwasting'. Rigveda 10.51: the dialogue: Varuna, 'who saw you hidden in the plants and waters?'; Agni, 'I fled in fear of the office; my elder brothers chose this road and died'; the gods, 'come, man is pious and waits; we give you a life that does not wear out'; Agni names his terms: the first offerings and the last, the fat of the waters, the long life of the gods.

Playbook: Animal in a supporting role (the fish, cursed to be eaten); burnout angle for today. Three texts tell one story; TS 2.6.6 is one long English entry, RV 10.51 is complete dialogue; BD 7.61 and 7.67 are empty in the corpus (skip). Pair with the epic Bhrigu-curses-Agni story.

Hindi hook draft: अग्नि के तीन बड़े भाई थे। तीनों देवताओं तक हवि पहुंचाते-पहुंचाते मर गए। तो अग्नि पानी में छिप गए।

title: A father left his son in the middle of the ocean 'as a dead man leaves his riches'.
angle: Tugra abandoned Bhujyu in the ocean, 'in the cloud of waters, where there is nothing to hold'. The twin gods came with ships that had a hundred oars. Kicker: The Ashvins were the two gods the other gods would not let drink Soma. They spent their time pulling people out of wells, pits and oceans. The Rigveda remembers the physicians better than their superiors.
notes:
Arc: Bhujyu, son of Tugra, is left in the sea (the hymns vary: a father's abandonment, a shipwreck); for three nights and three days the Ashvins carry him in winged ships, 'with a hundred oars', over the sea that gives no support, and set him on the shore. The same hymns list their other rescues: Rebha left for dead in a well for ten nights, Vandana buried, Atri thrown into the burning pit by the demons and kept cool.

Playbook: Rescue sequence with a father's betrayal as the opening image. Risk: the hymns are catalogues, so one protagonist (Bhujyu) must carry it and the others are the kicker's montage. Ashvins thread: also suryas-wedding, ghosha, dadhyanc, (published) sukanya.

title: In another Veda, Indra's dog took the bribe.
angle: You have seen Sarama find Indra's cows. The Brhaddevata has the ending the Rigveda left out: she drank the Panis' milk, and lied to Indra. Kicker: The channel's loyal dog has a second life in the Brahmanas, and in one of them loyalty failed. The Veda keeps both endings and never chooses.
notes:
Arc: The Panis hide the cows across the Rasa; Sarama crosses, refuses their offer of sisterhood (the RV dialogue), but then, by 'natural taste and greed', asks for milk, drinks it, returns, and tells Indra 'no' when he asks if she found the cows; Indra kicks her; she vomits the milk and confesses; Indra goes himself. The Jaiminiya version has her succeed, and Indra blesses her offspring: 'they shall be eaters of food'.

Playbook: Sequel/argument short (F11) built on the published Sarama hit; the audience knows the character. F6 caution: this is a 'but actually' structure by nature; open on the milk, not on 'you were told'. BD 8.30, 8.32-8.33, 8.35-8.36 are empty in the corpus; the key lines (8.31, 8.34) are present.

title: A sage became a bird to have children fast. Then he left them in the forest that was about to burn.
angle: Mandapala learned that heaven is closed to the childless. He became a bird, fathered four chicks in a week, and flew off with another female. Then Arjuna and Krishna set the Khandava forest on fire. Kicker: The longest dialogue in the burning of Khandava is not Arjuna's. It is four unborn birds arguing about whether their mother should live. The Mahabharata gives the smallest creatures the biggest question.
notes:
Arc: The four unhatched chicks are left with their mother Jarita; the fire comes; she offers to cover them with her body; the chicks, still featherless, debate: 'go, save yourself, you can have more sons'; one proposes the rat-hole, the others refuse ('the mongoose'); the mother flees; the chicks pray to Agni, who spares them because Mandapala had once praised him; the father returns; Jarita's speech to him is the sharpest in the chapter.

Playbook: Epic tier (Adi Parva). Animal + abandonment + loyalty; shares (F10). The Mandapala-Lapita subplot can be cut; keep the nest.

title: An old vulture fought a king for a woman he had met once.
angle: Jatayu was old enough to have been Dasharatha's friend. He saw Ravana's chariot and did not calculate. Kicker: Rama found Sita's trail because a bird refused to be too old for a fight. The epic's first funeral rite in exile was for a vulture.
notes:
Arc: Jatayu first argues with Ravana (the dharma of kings and guests), then attacks: breaks the chariot, kills the mules, tears the charioteer; Ravana cuts his wings. Rama finds him dying; he gives his report and dies; Rama performs his funeral as for a father.

Playbook: Epic tier (Aranya Kanda, Dutt). The two dog shorts were the channel's most-shared; loyal animals travel (F4). Dutt's 3.68 is the dying report, 3.69 the cremation ('I shall produce fire and burn the body of this king of birds').

title: Two sisters bet on the colour of a horse's tail. The loser's son became the king of birds.
angle: Kadru said the divine horse had a black tail. Vinata said white. The loser would be the other's slave. Kadru had a thousand snake sons, and told them to hang from the tail. Kicker: The Mahabharata's snakes-and-birds war began with a bet in the Veda, where the two sisters were Speech and Earth and the prize was Soma. The story grew a thousand snakes and a horse's tail; the bet is the same.
notes:
Arc: The snakes refuse to cheat; Kadru curses them to burn in Janamejaya's fire; some relent and hang from the tail as black hairs; Vinata loses and serves; her son Garuda is born, learns the price of freedom (the amrita), and the great heist begins. The Shatapatha has the Vedic seed: two 'illusions', Suparni and Kadru, bet on who sees farther across the ocean ('a white horse at a post; I see its tail waving'), and the loser must fetch Soma from heaven for the winner.

Playbook: Epic tier with a verified Vedic root (SB 3.6.2, English). Animal; family feud. Could be two shorts: the bet (above) and Garuda's heist (1.24-1.34). F9: 'why did the snakes get cursed by their own mother?' is in the text, say it.

title: He gave half his life to bring his bride back, and vowed to kill every frog. A frog talked him out of it.
angle: Pramadvara died of a snakebite the day before her wedding. Ruru begged the gods; a messenger said: give her half your life. He did. Then he picked up a stick. Kicker: The man who had just bought back his wife with half his life nearly spent the rest of it on revenge against animals. One snake with a human past stopped him.
notes:
Arc: Ruru revives Pramadvara at the cost of half his years and vows to kill every snake; he finds a dundubha (a harmless water-snake, a 'frog-eater'), raises his staff; the creature speaks: it was a Brahmin, Sahasrapat, cursed into this form for frightening a friend with a grass snake; it argues that killing the harmless is sin; Ruru relents; the curse lifts.

Playbook: Epic tier (Adi Parva, Pauloma). Animal + love; the 'frog' is a water-snake in Ganguli. Short enough for 90 s.

title: Before man, the gods tried living inside a cow. They said: not enough.
angle: The Self made the gods, and the gods fell into the great ocean, and Hunger and Thirst jumped on them. They asked for a body to live in. Kicker: Hunger is a god who lives where the gods live, by the oldest treaty in the Upanishads. That is why, the text says, you cannot feed a god without feeding hunger.
notes:
Arc: He brings them a cow: 'not sufficient for us'. A horse: 'not sufficient'. He brings them a human: 'O well made!' and they enter: fire as speech into the mouth, wind as breath, sun as sight. Then Hunger and Thirst ask: 'and where do we live?' 'Inside them, with the gods. Wherever an offering is made, you have a share.'

Playbook: Aitareya Upanishad 1-2 (short, complete in English). Animal as the rejected option; comedy of creation. Micro (60-75 s).

title: They called him a slave woman's son and sent him to die of thirst. The river followed him.
angle: At the sages' session on the Sarasvati, Kavasha sat down among them. 'Child of a slave woman. A cheat. No Brahmin. How did he get consecrated?' They sent him into the desert: let thirst kill him. Kicker: Two Vedas record that a slave woman's son was driven out by the Brahmins and that the holiest river in the Veda chose him. His hymn is in the Rigveda. Theirs, the text does not quote.
notes:
Arc: In the wilderness, dying of thirst, Kavasha Ailusha 'sees' the hymn to the Child of the Waters; the waters well up after him; the Sarasvati runs all around him (the place is still called Parisaraka, 'where she went around'). The seers: 'the gods know him; call him back.' They summon him and recite his hymn. The Kaushitaki version: 'we will not eat with you', and the river comes anyway.

Playbook: Defiance; caste; river as a character. Both passages complete in English. Strong F10 (injustice → shares) and F11 (comments). Do not editorialise beyond the text; the text is already the editorial.

Hindi hook draft: सरस्वती के किनारे ऋषियों के सत्र में कवष बैठ गया। 'दासी का बेटा। धोखेबाज़। ब्राह्मण नहीं।' उसे रेगिस्तान में भेज दिया: प्यास से मर जाए।

title: His brothers gave him nothing. His father gave him a trick worth a thousand cows.
angle: Nabhanedishtha came home from his studies to find his brothers had divided the property. 'What did you give me?' 'Him', they said, pointing at their father. Kicker: The disinherited son won twice: once with a hymn, once by admitting the cows were not his. The Brahmana says truth is a speech that wins a thousand.
notes:
Arc: The father: 'don't mind it; the Angirases are stuck on the sixth day of their sacrifice; teach them these two hymns and they will give you the thousand cows.' He does; they discern heaven and pay. As he gathers the herd, a man in black from the north claims it: 'what is left on the sacrificial ground is mine.' Father: 'it is his; but he will give it to you.' The boy goes back and says so; the man (Rudra) gives the thousand 'to you who spoke the truth'.

Playbook: One complete English passage; clean arc. The 'man in black from the north' is Rudra; show, don't name until the end.

title: Banned from the sacrifice, the outsider cited Indra's own exclusion to the king.
angle: King Vishvantara held a sacrifice without the Shyaparnas. They came anyway and sat down inside the altar. One of them opened his mouth. Kicker: The outsider's argument for being let in was that even Indra had once been thrown out. The Brahmana ends with the king pouring for him.
notes:
Arc: Rama Margaveya tells the king the story of Indra's exclusion by the gods (for misusing Vishvarupa, giving the ascetics to hyenas, breaking pacts) and how Indra still got his Soma back; he reasons that a king who sacrifices without the people who know will fail; the king relents and lets them drink.

Playbook: Defiance; pairs with indra-confession-pratardana (same list of Indra's crimes, AB 35.2). The passage is argumentative; keep the throne-room staging.

title: A boy bent in eight places walked into Janaka's court to free his father from the man who drowned losers.
angle: At Janaka's court, Bandin defeated every scholar in debate and had them drowned. One of them was a boy's father. The boy was twelve, and bent in eight places. Kicker: The boy who was mocked for his body won with arithmetic, and the first thing the father did with his freedom was fix the body. The Mahabharata lets you decide if that was necessary.
notes:
Arc: Ashtavakra, cursed in the womb for correcting his father's recitation, goes with his uncle Shvetaketu to Mithila; the gatekeeper mocks his age; he answers; the court laughs at his body; he answers ('a man is not old by grey hair'); the duel with Bandin is a numbers game (one fire, two friends, three Vedas... up to thirteen); Bandin fails at thirteen; the drowned scholars rise from the sea; the father bathes in a river and his son's body is made straight.

Playbook: Epic tier (Vana Parva). Defiance + disability + debate (comments). Note Shvetaketu, Uddalaka, Janaka: the Upanishad cast in an epic frame, a hook for the channel's Upanishad audience.

Hindi hook draft: जनक के दरबार में बंदी हर विद्वान को बहस में हराकर पानी में डुबवा देता था। उनमें एक लड़के का पिता भी था। लड़का बारह साल का था, आठ जगह से टेढ़ा।

title: It began with a dog that barked at the wrong man.
angle: The Pandavas' dog wandered into the forest and barked at a dark boy practising archery. Seven arrows closed its mouth without hurting it. That is how the princes found Ekalavya. Kicker: Everyone remembers the thumb. The epic's own first image is a dog that could not bark and was not bleeding. That was the skill Arjuna could never have.
notes:
Arc: The Nishada prince, refused by Drona, makes a clay Drona and learns from it; the dog's filled mouth reveals him; Arjuna complains; Drona asks for his fee: the right thumb; Ekalavya cuts it off, smiling, and keeps shooting, worse.

Playbook: Epic tier, universally known; the only reason to make it is the dog-first cut (F4) and the honesty of the kicker. Short section (one Ganguli chapter).

title: The gleaner was offered heaven in person. He asked for the terms, and said no.
angle: Mudgala lived on grain gleaned like a pigeon, and fed guests before himself. Durvasa came six times to eat everything he had. Then a messenger of the gods arrived with a chariot. Kicker: The epic's humblest man is the only one to interview heaven before accepting it, and the only one to turn it down.
notes:
Arc: Durvasa, the sage of rages, tests Mudgala's generosity by devouring his fortnight's grain repeatedly; Mudgala never flinches; heaven's messenger comes to take him up bodily; Mudgala asks what heaven is like; the messenger describes it honestly: the joy, and the fall when merit runs out, and the envy. Mudgala declines ('I do not want a place from which one falls') and goes on to seek the state beyond.

Playbook: Epic tier (Vana Parva). Defiance of a different kind; saves (F10 philosophy). Confirm the Ganguli section span; the story is Vana 260-261 in some numberings.

title: The ascetic who thought he was the most righteous man alive was sent to learn from a shopkeeper.
angle: Jajali stood so still in the forest that birds nested in his matted hair and raised their young. A voice said: you are not as righteous as Tuladhara, the grocer of Benares. Kicker: The sage with a bird's nest on his head learned ethics from a man weighing rice. The Mahabharata placed its sermon on non-violence in a shop.
notes:
Arc: Jajali goes to the market; Tuladhara, 'holder of the scales', already knows the story of the birds; he teaches harmlessness, fair weights, and that the man who hurts no creature outranks the man who hurts himself; Jajali objects, Tuladhara answers.

Playbook: Epic tier (Shanti Parva). Pairs with the Dharmavyadha (butcher) story; pick one. The bird-nest image is the hook.

title: A Brahmin was sent to learn dharma from a meat-seller in Mithila.
angle: A housewife told the proud Brahmin Kaushika she could not come at once because she was serving her husband; he lost his temper; she told him what he had done that morning. Then she sent him to a butcher. Kicker: The two best teachers in the Vana Parva are a wife at her chores and a man who sells meat. The Brahmin's whole journey was to learn he had parents.
notes:
Arc: Kaushika burnt a crane with his anger; the housewife knows it without being told; she sends him to Dharmavyadha, a fowler and meat-seller of Mithila, who explains how he lives righteously in a cruel trade, serves his parents, and reads the heart's dharma; Kaushika goes home to his own neglected parents.

Playbook: Epic tier (Vana Parva, ten long sections; cut to the housewife and the butcher's first speech). Caste, ethics; comments will be heavy (F11).

title: He wanted the Vedas without a teacher. Indra came as an old man throwing sand into the Ganga.
angle: Yavakri burned with austerities to get the Vedas directly from the gods, without studying. Indra refused. Then Indra appeared on the riverbank, an old man, pouring handfuls of sand into the Ganga to build a dam. Kicker: Indra, in this story, is the only sane person. The god the audience wants redeemed spends a whole chapter warning a young man, and is ignored.
notes:
Arc: 'You are mad, old man; you cannot dam the Ganga with sand.' 'No madder than you, trying to learn the Vedas without a teacher.' Yavakri persists; Indra grants it; the knowledge without discipline leads him to Raibhya's hermitage, the daughter-in-law, Raibhya's two demons from his hair, and his death; his father's grief; and Raibhya's own son kills his father by mistake; the chain is undone by Brhadadyumna's boon.

Playbook: Epic tier (Vana Parva). Indra series crossover and a 'student' story for the Upanishad audience. The sexual-assault element (Yavakri and Raibhya's daughter-in-law) must be handled as the text does, briefly, or the cut ends at the dam.

title: In a famine he ate a stranger's leftover beans and refused the water. Then he crashed a king's sacrifice.
angle: Hail had destroyed the Kuru crops. Ushasti and his child-wife were starving in an elephant-driver's village. The driver was eating beans. Kicker: The Upanishad that teaches the secret of the chant opens with a man explaining why eating a stranger's leftovers is not a sin and drinking his water is. Hunger has rules, and the rules have reasons.
notes:
Arc: Ushasti begs; the driver says 'only these, which I have begun eating'; 'give me them'; he eats the leftovers but refuses the leftover water: 'eating these I could not have lived; water I can get anywhere.' He keeps some beans for his wife; she has already begged her own, saves his. Next morning he hears a king's sacrifice is on, walks in, and tells the three chief priests that if they chant without knowing the deity of their chant, their heads will fall off; the king makes him chief priest; he teaches the three deities (breath, sun, food).

Playbook: Complete in English (Ch 1.10-1.11). F1: a protagonist with a want and a turn. F9: 'why refuse water but eat the beans?' is the text's own point; make it the mid-story question. The three 'heads will fall off' threats echo Gargi (see gargi-two-arrows).

Hindi hook draft: ओलों ने कुरु देश की फ़सल खत्म कर दी थी। उषस्ति और उसकी बाल-पत्नी एक महावत के गांव में भूखे थे। महावत बीन्स खा रहा था।

title: The teacher left him behind. So the sacred fires taught him themselves.
angle: Upakosala tended his teacher's fires for twelve years. Every other student was sent home with the knowledge. He was not. Kicker: The published Satyakama was taught by a bull, a fire, a swan and a bird. His own student had to be taught by the fires because Satyakama, of all people, held back. The Upanishads do not pretend good students make good teachers.
notes:
Arc: Satyakama (himself the boy who did not know his father) lets his other pupils go but withholds from Upakosala; the teacher's wife pleads; Satyakama goes away without teaching; the boy stops eating; the three fires take pity and teach him 'breath is Brahman'; each fire adds its lesson; when Satyakama returns he sees the boy's face shining 'like one who knows Brahman': 'who taught you?' 'The fires.' 'They told you the worlds; I will tell you the way.'

Playbook: Direct sequel to the queued satyakama short (Ch 4.4-4.9); make them a pair. The teacher's-wife line is the turn.

title: He had learnt everything from his father. A king asked him five questions. He knew none.
angle: Shvetaketu came to the Panchala court sure of himself. The king asked: do you know where creatures go after death? How they come back? Where the two roads part? Why the other world never fills up? How water becomes a man? Five times: no. Kicker: The most famous father-son teaching pair in the Upanishads got their best lesson by being humiliated by a king who then told them Brahmins had never owned it. The text wrote that down about itself.
notes:
Arc: The boy goes home angry: 'you said you taught me everything'; the father admits he does not know either and goes to the king as a pupil; the king offers wealth; Uddalaka asks for the knowledge; the king says 'this knowledge has never before gone to a Brahmin; among all peoples it belonged to the kshatriya' and teaches the five fires and the two paths.

Playbook: Also BU 6.2 (same story). 29 entries; script the five questions as a drumbeat (guide §2 refrain). F11 flavour: 'the kshatriya's knowledge' line will drive comments; keep it as the text's claim.

Hindi hook draft: श्वेतकेतु पांचाल दरबार में पहुंचा, अपने ज्ञान पर पक्का। राजा ने पूछा: मरकर प्राणी कहां जाते हैं? लौटते कैसे हैं? दो रास्ते कहां बंटते हैं? परलोक भरता क्यों नहीं? पानी इंसान कैसे बनता है? पांच बार: पता नहीं।

title: Twelve years of Veda made him arrogant. His father fixed it with a fruit and a glass of salt water.
angle: Shvetaketu came home at twenty-four, 'conceited, thinking himself learned'. His father asked: did you ask for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard? Kicker: 'Tat tvam asi' is repeated nine times in the text, every time after an object: a seed, salt, a river, a blindfolded man. The Upanishad did not want it believed. It wanted it tasted.
notes:
Arc: Uddalaka: 'bring a banyan fruit; break it; what do you see? seeds; break one; what do you see? nothing. From that nothing this great tree. That is the self. You are that.' 'Put this salt in water; bring it tomorrow; find the salt. Taste the top, the middle, the bottom.' 'It is salt everywhere.' 'So the being you cannot see is in all of this. You are that.' The last image: a man blindfolded, led from his home and left in the forest, asking his way village by village.

Playbook: Three short ranges instead of the whole 69-entry chapter. The published Indra-Virochana used the same father-pupil 'return with doubt' rhythm; this is the companion with concrete demonstrations (guide §4: concrete images before the summing line).

Hindi hook draft: श्वेतकेतु चौबीस साल का होकर लौटा, घमंडी, खुद को विद्वान समझता। पिता ने पूछा: वो शिक्षा मांगी, जिससे अनसुना सुना हो जाता है?

title: Three sages met a king on the road. He out-argued them. One of them ran after his chariot.
angle: Janaka asked three travelling Brahmins how each performed the fire offering. Each answered. Each was wrong, the king explained, and drove on. Kicker: The sage who later took Janaka's thousand cows without a debate first lost to him on a road, and ran behind his chariot to say so.
notes:
Arc: Shvetaketu, Somashushma and Yajnavalkya each describe their Agnihotra; Janaka shows how each falls short; 'this fellow of a Rajanya has out-talked us; let us challenge him'; Yajnavalkya: 'we are Brahmins; he is a kshatriya; if we lose we will be the laughing-stock'; he runs after Janaka's chariot alone and asks to learn; Janaka teaches where the two libations go (air, sky, earth, man, woman) and grants him a boon; Yajnavalkya, who had refused to be taught by a king, becomes his man. (BU 4.3 continues: 'from then Janaka was a Brahmin', jokes Yajnavalkya.)

Playbook: Companion to gargi-two-arrows (same two men, earlier). JB 1.22-1.26 has a parallel (five Brahmins plot to beat Janaka); SB 11.6.2 is the clean version.

title: The proud scholar offered to teach the king. The king paid a thousand cows and then taught him.
angle: Gargya Balaki, who had travelled every kingdom, came to Ajatashatru of Kashi: 'Shall I tell you Brahman?' The king: 'A thousand cows for that speech, for people run to Janaka and leave us.' Kicker: The king's lesson was not a speech. It was a man asleep and a stick. The Upanishad says the Brahmin came as a teacher and 'with fuel in hand', as a pupil, went home.
notes:
Arc: Balaki offers sixteen definitions (the person in the sun, the moon, lightning, the mirror, the shadow, the echo, the dream); the king rejects each 'do not make me talk about him'; Balaki falls silent; 'so much only?' The king takes him by the hand to a sleeping man, calls him by names; he does not wake; strikes him with a stick; he wakes. 'Where was he? Where did he come back from?' And teaches the self in sleep and the veins of the heart.

Playbook: Twenty short entries; BU 2.1 parallel. The sixteen definitions must become a quick montage (three or four), not a list (F1 leak).

title: A king asked the priest's son one question. The priest's son went home. The priest came back as a student.
angle: Citra Gangyayani asked young Shvetaketu, come to be his priest: is there a closed door in the world where you will put me, or a road on? 'I don't know; let me ask my teacher.' Kicker: In this Upanishad death is an interview conducted by the moon, and the only passing answer is a sentence. The teacher of the greatest Upanishadic father was a king.
notes:
Arc: The father, Aruni, admits he does not know either; both go to the king with fuel in hand; the king, pleased: 'you are worthy'. He teaches: all who leave this world go to the moon; the moon asks each 'who are you?'; those who cannot answer are rained back into life; the one who answers 'I am you' passes the moon, to the river Vijara, the tree Ilya, the city Salajja, the throne Vicakshana, where Brahman asks 'who are you?' again.

Playbook: Kaushitaki 1 (six entries, English). Visual-rich afterlife itinerary (the river, the tree, the couch). F9: 'why the moon?' is unanswered in the text; say so.

title: The thunder said one syllable. Gods, men and demons each heard a different word.
angle: Three classes of Prajapati's children finished their studies and asked their father for a last teaching. He said: Da. Kicker: One syllable, three listeners, three commands, and each heard the one it needed. The Upanishad's shortest lesson is the one the thunder still gives.
notes:
Arc: The gods: 'you said damyata, control yourselves; yes.' Men: 'you said datta, give; yes.' The demons: 'you said dayadhvam, be compassionate; yes.' 'This the divine voice, the thunder, repeats: da, da, da.'

Playbook: Micro (45-60 s). T. S. Eliot ended The Waste Land with it; a pinned-comment fact, not a line in the short.

title: Five times he came back with an answer. Five times his father said: go and think again.
angle: Bhrigu asked his father Varuna: teach me Brahman. Varuna named the hints (food, breath, eye, ear, mind) and sent him away to find it himself. Kicker: The same Bhrigu, in another text, is sent by his father to see hell (the queued short). Here the father sends him to think, five times, and never once tells him the answer. The Taittiriya says that is the teaching.
notes:
Arc: Bhrigu does tapas, returns: 'food is Brahman, from food all are born'; 'go, think again'; 'breath'; 'again'; 'mind'; 'again'; 'knowledge'; 'again'; 'bliss', and there the text stops asking him to return. Then the practical rules: do not blame food; do not reject food; heap food; welcome the guest.

Playbook: Complete in English (TU 3). Same refrain rhythm that worked in Indra-Virochana (return with doubt). Companion to the queued bhrigu-other-world (JB/SB) as a two-part 'Varuna's son'.

title: The gods could not burn, lift or recognise a blade of grass. A woman told them why.
angle: The gods had won. 'Ours is the victory.' Something appeared before them they did not know. They sent Agni to find out what it was. Kicker: The three greatest gods were defeated by a blade of grass, and the only one who knew what had happened was the woman standing where it had been. The Kena Upanishad puts her name before Indra's.
notes:
Arc: 'Who are you?' 'I am Agni, I can burn anything.' It lays a blade of grass before him: 'burn this.' He cannot. Vayu: 'I can carry anything away.' He cannot move it. Indra goes; it vanishes; in that place he sees a woman, Uma, daughter of the mountain, and asks her; she says: 'it was Brahman; by its victory you were victorious.' So Indra 'touched it nearest', and Agni and Vayu after him.

Playbook: Short (Kena 3-4, 21 entries), complete, vivid. Devotional plus (Uma). Indra series side-note: Indra is 'first among gods' because he was the one who went to ask.

Hindi hook draft: देवता जीत गए थे। 'हमारी जीत है।' तभी सामने कुछ प्रकट हुआ, जिसे वे पहचान नहीं पाए। उन्होंने अग्नि को भेजा: पता करो, ये क्या है।

title: He knew every science there was. He came to say he was still sad.
angle: Narada listed the Vedas, history, grammar, mathematics, logic, astrology, snake-charming, the fine arts: 'all this I know, sir; I know the words. I am a knower of words only, not a knower of the Self. I have heard that the knower of the Self crosses sorrow. I am in sorrow.' Kicker: The first thing the Upanishad asks of its most learned student is a list of what his learning has failed to fix. Then it does not add a subject. It subtracts.
notes:
Arc: Sanatkumara leads him up a ladder: name, speech, mind, will, memory, hope, breath... each 'greater' than the last, to the Infinite, 'where one sees nothing else'; and the last line, 'the pure in food, the pure in nature; Narada's darkness destroyed'.

Playbook: Doctrine-heavy; the 'I am sad' confession and the syllabus list are the only dramatic beats. Better as a 60-s hook-and-kicker piece than a full arc; or as a pinned-comment reply to 'how to start reading the Vedas'.

title: Six scholars went to a king for knowledge. He began by listing what his kingdom did not have.
angle: 'In my kingdom there is no thief, no miser, no drunkard, no man without a sacred fire, no ignorant man, no adulterer, so how could there be an adulteress?' Then Ashvapati taught the six what each of them had been worshipping as the whole. Kicker: A king's boast about law and order is the preface to the Upanishad's lesson that everyone's god is a body part.
notes:
Arc: Six great householders cannot agree what the universal Self is; they go to Uddalaka, who sends them to King Ashvapati; the king boasts of his kingdom, then shows each man that his 'self' (sky, sun, wind, space, water, earth) is only the head, eye, breath, trunk, bladder or feet of one being.

Playbook: Thin arc (F1 leak risk: six answers in a row). Keep only if the producer wants a 'king teaches Brahmins' mini-series with shvetaketu-five-questions and balaki-and-ajatashatru.

title: A king gave away his kingdom, stood in the sun for a thousand days with his arms raised, and asked what a body is for.
angle: 'What is the use of pleasure in this body, a mass of bones, skin, sinews, marrow, flesh, seed, blood, mucus, tears, phlegm, ordure, bile and slime?' Kicker: The Maitri Upanishad's catalogue of vanished kings reads like a roll-call of the channel's own stories: Marutta, Bharata, Sudyumna. The king asking the question had read them too.
notes:
Arc: Brihadratha installs his son, goes to the forest, stands facing the sun with arms up; Shakayanya appears; the king's speech lists the body's parts and the names of dead emperors (Sudyumna, Bhuridyumna, Marutta, Bharata...) who had to leave it all; the sage agrees to teach the Self.

Playbook: Mood piece with a strong monologue, weak arc (constitution rule 6). Use the body-list as a cold open for another short, or skip.

title: The son called his father 'grey-haired' to his face for serving three rival kings.
angle: Jabala Aruni became chaplain to three competing kings at once, Kashi, Kosala and the Ikshvaku, and grew rich. His son Shvetaketu said: grey-haired one, you match others in fame, never yourself. Kicker: Even in the Brahmanas the famous son of the famous father was a brat. The same Shvetaketu is humiliated by a king in the Chandogya, which may be why.
notes:
Arc: The father: 'do not speak so to me; the rite was known to me; you, like a wretched pseudo-Brahmin, tried to find it out; it was as they taught me, and even more.' Then the text turns to the gods outwitting Death.

Playbook: Micro only; one entry. Feeds the Shvetaketu thread (salt, five questions, Ashtavakra's uncle).

title: Six seekers came with questions. The teacher made them wait a year before asking.
angle: 'Live another year in austerity and faith; then ask what you will, and if I know, I will hide nothing.' Kicker: The Prashna Upanishad's first teaching is the year of silence before the first question. The questions are the second teaching.
notes:
Arc: Six named students (Sukesha, Satyakama, Gargya, Kaushalya, Bhargava, Kabandhi) wait a year with Pippalada; then the first question: where do creatures come from? And the answer: the Creator made a pair, breath and matter, the sun and the moon.

Playbook: Micro; no conflict. Keep only as an interstitial or a pinned comment on 'how to start reading the Vedas'.

title: The demons were dividing the earth. The gods sent a dwarf to ask for 'as much as he can lie on'.
angle: The Asuras had won the earth and were measuring it out with ox-hides, west to east. The gods came to beg a share. Kicker: In the Shatapatha the dwarf is the gods' con, not an avatar: the earth was won by sacrifice, not by three steps. The three steps come later, from the same seed.
notes:
Arc: 'As much as this Vishnu lies on.' 'Now Vishnu was a dwarf.' The Asuras, not offended, give it; the gods lay him down, enclose him on three sides with the metres and fire on the fourth, and by that 'sacrifice' win the whole earth. Then Vishnu, tired, hides in the roots of the plants; the gods dig for him. The Taittiriya adds that Vishnu 'saw' the dwarf and offered it to its own deity.

Playbook: F6 warning: do not open with 'you think Vamana was Vishnu's avatar, but...'. Open on the Asuras measuring with hides. Devotional sensitivity moderate; the text is the Veda's own Vamana.

title: The demons lost because they fed only themselves.
angle: Gods and demons, both children of Prajapati, strove. The demons, in arrogance, said: 'to whom should we offer?' and put the offerings into their own mouths. Kicker: The Veda's shortest explanation of why the demons lost: they ate what they should have given. Two sentences, one rule.
notes:
Arc: The gods went on offering to one another; Prajapati gave himself up to them; so they became the sacrifice and won. 'Wherefore let no one be arrogant, for verily arrogance is the cause of ruin.'

Playbook: Micro (30-45 s), perfect as a series bumper or a reel with one image (two tables). Also at SB 11.1.8.1.

title: The newborn god cried until his father gave him a name. Then he wanted another. Eight times.
