angle: Prajapati's son was born crying. 'My boy, why do you cry?' 'I have not been given a name. Give me a name.' Kicker: Shiva's first word was a complaint, and his first eight names were extracted from a father one at a time. The Veda's fiercest god began as a baby who would not stop until he had the whole world.
notes:
Arc: 'You are Rudra.' The boy: 'I am greater than that; give me another.' 'Sharva.' 'Pashupati.' 'Ugra.' 'Ashani.' 'Bhava.' 'Mahan Deva.' 'Ishana.' Each name makes a part of the world his: fire, water, plants, wind, lightning, rain, moon, sun. 'These are the eight forms of Agni; Kumara, the boy, is the ninth.' (The Kaushitaki version: 'without a name I cannot eat food here.')

Playbook: Devotional plus; micro-to-short (75-90 s). Note that the text calls the boy Agni/Kumara; the names are the Rudra names. KB 6.1-6.3 has the fuller 'cannot eat without a name' dialogue if the producer wants it.

Hindi hook draft: प्रजापति का बेटा रोता हुआ पैदा हुआ। 'बेटा, रोते क्यों हो?' 'मुझे नाम नहीं मिला। मुझे नाम दो।'

title: The gods created two illusions and made them bet.
angle: Soma was in heaven; the gods were here. So they created Suparni and Kadru, who were Speech and Earth, and set them quarrelling. Kicker: The Mahabharata turned this into Kadru and Vinata, a thousand snakes and Garuda. In the Veda the two sisters were a trick the gods played on themselves to get Soma down to earth.
notes:
Arc: 'Who sees farther?' Suparni: 'a white horse at a post across the ocean.' Kadru: 'I see its tail waving.' 'Fly and check.' Suparni flies; Kadru was right; 'I have won your own self; fetch me Soma from heaven.' Suparni sends her children (the metres) for Soma, which is enclosed in two sharp golden cups closing every blink.

Playbook: Vedic root of kadru-vinata-bet (epic tier); make the epic one first and this as the 'where it came from' follow-up, or fold into one. Short and complete.

title: The gods built a god to punish their father. He became the hunter in the sky.
angle: Prajapati desired his own daughter, the Dawn. He became a stag; she a doe. The gods said: this is a sin; who among us can punish him? And they found no one. Kicker: Look up in winter: the Veda says the three stars of Orion's belt are an arrow still in the body of the creator, fired by a god made for one job. Punishment, in the Veda, is written on the sky.
notes:
Arc: They pour their most terrible forms together and make a god (Bhutavat, Rudra); he pierces Prajapati with an arrow; Prajapati becomes the deer in the sky (Mriga, the Orion stars), the arrow is the belt, the archer the star Mrigavyadha; the seed falls and becomes the lake Sharyanavat, the Adityas, the Angirases. The Shatapatha quotes the Rigveda verse about it.

Playbook: High devotional sensitivity (Prajapati-daughter incest as the text states it). Astronomy angle is the safe entry (the channel's audience asked for 'mythological beings'). AB 13.9 is complete; SB 1.7.4.1-4 gives the arrow/Rudra. Producer decision.

title: Death stalked the gods from chant to chant. They ran to their father.
angle: 'They are chanting the Trivrt,' thought Death, and went to wait for them at the next chant. They went around him. Kicker: The Jaiminiya describes a sacrifice as a chase scene. Death is the one who gets lost.
notes:
Arc: The gods sing a sequence of stomas; Death moves ahead to each; they take refuge in the Vishvajit, in Prajapati; 'having outwitted Death they went to heaven'. Thus the ten-day rite is 'the outwitting of Death'.

Playbook: Ritual allegory; only as a 30-s bumper or an image for another short.

title: Indra and Agni won the race. That is why they get the cake.
angle: Creatures were starving. The gods found the sap of heaven and earth and could not agree whose it was. So they raced for it. Kicker: The oldest tie-breaker in Indian theology was a footrace.
notes:
Arc: Each god claims it ('mine!'); they agree 'whoever beats the others, his it shall be'; Indra and Agni win; hence the twelve-potsherd cake for Indra-Agni at the seasonal offering.

Playbook: Micro; combine with suryas-wedding-donkey-race as 'the gods' races'.

title: Ten kings against one, at a river. The oldest war in Indian history has a hymn.
angle: Ten kings crossed the Parushni to crush Sudas. The river was the ally that turned. Kicker: The channel has told the stories of priests and demons. This one has a date-able king, named enemies, a river that drowned an army, and a poet on the winning side writing his own fee into the last verse.
notes:
Arc: 7.18: Vasishtha's victory hymn: the Turvashas, Yakshus, Matsyas, Bhrigus, Druhyus, the Purus, Anus 'desiring plunder like unfed fish', 'Indra made the ford easy for Sudas and the waters hard for the enemy'; the Anu king's armour and chariot taken; Bheda's fall; the sixty-six thousand slain, 'as a cow kicks her calf'; the kings' names, the priests Vasishtha in white robes (7.33). 7.83: Indra and Varuna 'heard Sudas in the battle of ten kings'.

Playbook: History angle (the audience asked for 'how to start reading the Vedas'; this is where historians start). Griffith's 7.18 is readable but dense; the writer should pick six concrete verses (the fish, the ford, the armour, the calf, the fee). 7.33 adds Vasishtha's sons in white. Risk: list of tribes (F1 leak); keep to three names.

Hindi hook draft: दस राजा सुदास को कुचलने परुष्णी नदी पार कर आए। नदी ही वो साथी थी, जो पलट गई।

title: King Sudas's heir killed Vasishtha's hundred sons. The sage wrote a curse, and a confession.
angle: The sage who won Sudas his war lost his hundred sons to Sudas's descendants. The Rigveda keeps the hymn he wrote that night. Kicker: The Rigveda's most famous curse against demons contains a father swearing he is not one. Grief, in the Veda, had to prove its innocence before it could ask for revenge.
notes:
Arc: Brhaddevata: Vasishtha, his hundred sons slain by the Saudasas (Sudas's line, under a curse), 'full of pain', saw the demon-killing hymn 7.104 ('Indra and Soma, burn the fiends'), and in it says, as if accused of being a sorcerer himself: 'if I am a demon, if I have harmed a man, may I die today'. The Kaushitaki records the 'Vasishtha sacrifice' he saw to 'overcome the Saudasas' and win offspring again.

Playbook: Seer feud (Vasishtha-Vishvamitra via Shakti, BD 4.112, is truncated in the corpus). BD 6.31-6.32 empty; 6.28, 6.33, 6.34 carry the frame. 7.104 is complete (25 verses). The later Kalmashapada/Saudasa tale is Mahabharata (Adi 176-177), not in the Vedic packet; flag as later.

title: 'What was my sin, Varuna? I once rode in your boat.' A sage's confession, in his own voice.
angle: Vasishtha had been Varuna's friend; they had sailed together on the god's ship and 'the sun rose on us both'. Now he is sick, bound, and asking what he did. Kicker: The oldest first-person prayer of a man who does not know what he did wrong. Three thousand years before 'guilt' had a word in psychology, a sage listed the four excuses: wine, dice, anger, a dream.
notes:
Arc: 7.86: 'I ask the wise what my sin was; they say Varuna is angry with you'; 'it was not my will but wine, dice, anger, a dream'; 'free us from our fathers' sins and our own'. 7.88: the memory of the boat. 7.89: 'let me not go to the house of clay; if I have wronged you it was through weakness; have mercy'.

Playbook: Emotion (F10: shares) but no plot; build the arc from the boat (friendship) to the clay house (illness) to the plea. The two published hits are both story-first; test this as the 'inner' short. Companion: the queued gambler's lament (10.34).

title: The elder brother had a skin disease, so he gave the throne to Shantanu. Then it stopped raining.
angle: Shantanu, Bhishma's father, had an elder brother. The Rigveda remembers him: Devapi, who refused the crown and went to the forest. Twelve years without rain followed. Kicker: The Mahabharata mentions Devapi in a line. The Rigveda has his hymn: the sick elder brother asking the gods for rain for the brother he gave the kingdom to. The Kuru story begins in the Veda with a man refusing a throne.
notes:
Arc: Brhaddevata: Devapi, afflicted with skin disease, declares himself unfit; Shantanu is anointed; Parjanya withholds rain; the Brahmins say the younger brother was wrongly made king while the elder lived; Shantanu goes to the forest and offers the crown back; Devapi refuses again but agrees to be his priest; he sacrifices with the hymn 10.98 ('Brhaspati, be Mitra, Varuna, Pushan; place brilliant speech in my mouth'), and the rain falls.

Playbook: Mahabharata root (the published Dog short proved this audience likes Vedic roots of the epic). BD 7.155, 7.157, 8.1, 8.4, 8.6, 8.8, 8.9 are truncated/empty in the corpus; 7.156, 8.2, 8.3, 8.5, 8.7 carry the plot; RV 10.98 is complete. Also in Nirukta 2.10 (no English in corpus) and Yaska's story matches.

Hindi hook draft: शांतनु, यानी भीष्म के पिता, के एक बड़े भाई थे। ऋग्वेद उन्हें याद रखता है: देवापि, जिन्होंने राज ठुकराया और जंगल चले गए। फिर बारह साल बारिश नहीं हुई।

title: The king's chariot killed a Brahmin boy. The king blamed the priest. The priest blamed the king.
angle: King Tryaruna was driving; his chaplain Vrisha held the reins. A boy was cut down. Whose fault, the driver's or the one who told him to go fast? Kicker: The Rigveda's hymn 5.2 begins 'a young mother hides the boy' and no one knew why until the Brhaddevata told the story: a wrongful death, a priest's strike, and a kingdom whose fire went out.
notes:
Arc: Each blames the other; the Ikshvakus are asked to judge; they side with the king; Vrisha revives the boy with Atharvan spells and leaves; the fire in the king's house dies with him; the king comes begging; Vrisha returns and finds the 'heat' hidden by a Pishachi, the king's wife's demon, under a cushion; he recovers it with the verse 'whom do you hide, as a boy?' (RV 5.2).

Playbook: Justice theme (F10 injustice). BD 5.19, 5.21, 5.22 truncated/empty; 5.14-5.18, 5.20 intact. RV 5.2 is complete but cryptic; the BD frame is the story.

title: He wanted the princess. The king said: only a seer may marry her. So he became one.
angle: At King Rathaviti's sacrifice, the young priest Shyavashva saw the king's daughter. The king was willing. The queen asked: is he a rishi? Kicker: The Rigveda's hymns 5.52 to 5.61 exist because a boy was told he was not good enough for a princess. The Maruts, gods of storm, were his tutors in the art of becoming good enough.
notes:
Arc: He is not; the match is refused; Shyavashva wanders, is blessed by Queen Shashiyasi, meets the Maruts on the road and praises them; they make him a seer; he composes the hymns to the Maruts (5.52-5.61) and sends a message to the king through the night (5.61: 'tell Rathaviti...'); the king gives his daughter.

Playbook: Romance; the only one in the corpus with a clean rom-com shape. BD 5.50-5.80 is 32 entries and several are empty in the corpus (5.81 blank); the writer must work from the intact ones (5.50, 5.55, 5.56, 5.60, 5.65 confirmed). RV 5.61 carries the message to the king.

title: A student fell asleep on the road home. He woke up married to ten princesses.
angle: Kakshivat, son of a slave-woman and the blind sage Dirghatamas, walked home from his studies, lay down in the forest and slept. King Svanaya found him 'like the son of a god'. Kicker: Not every seer in the Rigveda earned his hymns by austerity. One slept well in the right forest. His hymn is a thank-you note.
notes:
Arc: The king asks his lineage, marries him to his ten daughters, gives a hundred necklets, a hundred bulls, horses, ten chariots; Kakshivat praises him in 1.125-1.126 ('at morn the giver of a hundred came'); his father Dirghatamas blesses the gift.

Playbook: Sparse but intact (BD 3.142-3.150, except 3.147). Dirghatamas (blind from birth; thrown in the Ganga in later texts) is only glancingly in the corpus (BD 4.15 'suddenly blind'); not enough for his own short.

title: The fish prayed to the gods from the dry land, and the fishermen let them go.
angle: Fishermen on the Sarasvati cast a net, caught the fish and threw them on the bank. The fish, frightened, praised the sons of Aditi. Kicker: A Rigvedic hymn attributed to fish. The channel's two dog shorts were its biggest. This is the aquatic sequel.
notes:
Arc: The Adityas release them, and tell the fishermen: do not fear hunger; you will reach heaven. The hymn 8.67 ('let not Vivasvat's net destroy us before old age') is, the Brhaddevata says, the fishes' hymn.

Playbook: Micro, charming, thin; 8.67 (the corpus has Wilson's rendering for this hymn) is long for a fish prayer. Pair with agni-quit-fish-told in a 'fish in the Veda' pinned comment.

title: A year of silence, then the rains, and the frogs sang like priests. The Rigveda meant it as a compliment.
angle: 'Like Brahmins who have kept their vows, the frogs lay quiet for a year. Then the rains came, and they lifted up their voice.' Kicker: The hymn was sung to bring rain, and the only priests in it are frogs. Vasishtha's family kept it in the family book. The channel's audience will decide whether it is satire; the text has been letting people decide for three thousand years.
notes:
Arc: Each frog answers the other 'as a pupil repeats the teacher'; Cow-bellow and Goat-bleat, Green and Spotty, croak in turn 'as Brahmins round the Soma vessel at the all-night rite'; 'they keep the twelve-month order; they never neglect the season'; and in the last verse they grant cattle and long life.

Playbook: No protagonist; the arc is the year (silence, first drop, chorus). Treat like the Vratyas short (an explainer with a twist), expect Vratya-like retention (F1), but the animal comedy may out-share it (F4). Ten verses, complete.

title: 'I'm a poet. Dad's a doctor. Mum grinds corn.' The Rigveda's hymn on jobs.
angle: We all have different plans: the carpenter wants a crack, the doctor a patient, the priest a sponsor. 'A bard am I, my dad's a leech, mammy lays corn upon the stones.' Kicker: The oldest 'what does your family do' in Indian literature, and the family is mixed: poet, physician, miller. Caste, in this hymn, is three jobs in one house.
notes:
Arc: Four verses: trades and desires (the smith, the horse that wants an easy cart, the frog that wants water), ending 'flow, Soma, for Indra'.

Playbook: Micro (45 s); argument-short flavour (F11) on occupations and caste. The published 'professions in the Yajurveda' covered the Purushamedha list; this is the personal version.

title: A child made a chariot with no wheels and rode it to Yama's tree.
angle: 'In the tree with fair leaves where Yama drinks with the gods, the father looks after the men of old.' A child has followed him. Kicker: Nachiketa, who went to Death's house, has a nameless forerunner: a child in Rigveda 10.135 who built his own chariot to go there. The Veda did not explain it. The Katha Upanishad did.
notes:
Arc: The child mounts a wheel-less car he made in his mind; the Saman follows it; 'who was the father of the child? who made the car roll?'; the funeral gift is placed; the point of flame appears; 'here is the seat where Yama dwells'.

Playbook: Cryptic hymn; the queued Nachiketa short should mention it in the pinned comment rather than this being its own short.

title: A possessed woman was asked: where did the Parikshitas go? The Upanishad records the answer.
angle: At Janaka's debate, Bhujyu told Yajnavalkya: we were travelling in Madra, in the house of Patanchala Kapya, whose daughter was possessed by a Gandharva. We asked it who it was, and we asked it: where did the Parikshitas go? Kicker: The Mahabharata's royal family, the Parikshitas, were already a lost dynasty when the Upanishads were composed. People asked spirits where they had gone. That is how old the Kurus are.
notes:
Arc: The Gandharva (in 3.3) says 'they went where the horse-sacrificers go', and the question is thrown at Yajnavalkya: where is that? He answers with the size of the world, thirty-two days of the sun's chariot, and the winds that carry the sacrificers beyond it. In 3.7 another Gandharva, possessing the same household's wife, asks about the 'thread' that holds the worlds together.

Playbook: Mahabharata root (the published Dog short cited Sarama's curse on Janamejaya; this is the same family). The BU translation in the corpus carries Shankara's commentary; take only the narrative sentences. Also SB 11.5.5.13 ('the palace of Janamejaya') and AB 39.7 (Janamejaya's horse sacrifice at Asandivant) can be cited.

Hindi hook draft: जनक की सभा में भुज्यु ने याज्ञवल्क्य से कहा: हम मद्र देश में पतंचल काप्य के घर ठहरे थे। उनकी बेटी पर एक गंधर्व सवार था। हमने उससे पूछा: परीक्षित के वंशज कहां गए?

title: Seven kings were anointed like Indra. When one tried to give away the Earth, the Earth sang back.
angle: With the 'great anointing of Indra', Tura Kavasheya anointed Janamejaya, Vasishtha anointed Sudas, Dirghatamas anointed Bharata. Each went round the earth conquering. Then Vishvakarman Bhauvana tried to give the earth itself to his priest. Kicker: The land is named after one king on this list. The list's only speaking character is the land, refusing to be a gift.
notes:
Arc: The Aitareya's roll of anointed kings: Janamejaya Parikshita (the horse at Asandivant 'with a yellow garland'), Sharyata, Shatanika, Ambashthya, Yudhamshraushti, Vishvakarman, Sudas, Marutta, Anga, Bharata Daushyanti (133 horses by the Yamuna and the Ganga, 'no man can reach his deeds, as no man can seize the sky with his hands'); and the Earth singing to Vishvakarman: 'No man whatsoever ought to give me; you wished to give me; I shall plunge into the middle of the waters; vain was your compact with Kashyapa.'

Playbook: Explainer risk (a list of kings); the arc is Vishvakarman's gift and the Earth's refusal, with Janamejaya and Bharata as the frame. The published 'Mahabharata dog' audience and the docs/mahabharata_references note in this repo back the angle.

title: 'Which shall I cook for you, curds or barley brew?' the wife asks, in the kingdom of King Parikshit.
angle: The Atharvaveda has a jingle about a king: 'under Parikshit the ripe barley springs up, the people thrive, a Kauravya says to his wife...' It is the Mahabharata's Parikshit, or his ancestor, and it is the oldest mention of the Kurus by name. Kicker: A kitchen conversation is the oldest surviving portrait of Kuru rule. Not a battle. A wife asking what to cook.
notes:
Arc: Four verses: the king 'excelling mortals like a god'; the husband 'ordering his house' says the king has given rest; the wife asks what to serve, curds, milk-gruel or barley-brew; the barley springs 'up to the cleft'.

Playbook: Micro (45-60 s), a 'Mahabharata root' bumper; cite docs/mahabharata_references_in_vedic_texts.md in this repo for the Devanagari. F6: don't open on 'before the Mahabharata'; open on the wife's question.

title: King Soma took a Brahmin's wife. The gods made him give her back.
angle: The Brahmin's wife, the hymn says, was taken; the gods and the Seven Seers sat in austerity until King Soma 'without reluctance made restitution'. Kicker: The Puranic Tara, taken by the moon from Brhaspati, has her seed here, in a hymn that is a verdict: give her back.
notes:
Arc: Seven verses: the gods' decree that the Brahmin's wife must be returned, 'the kings who kept their promise' restoring her, the ones who shared the bribe freed from sin.

Playbook: Micro; thin. Only if the producer builds a 'where Puranic stories come from' series.

title: The Rigveda's creation hymn ends with: he who is highest in heaven knows. Or maybe he does not.
angle: 'Then there was neither death nor immortality, nor night nor day. Who knows whence it came? The gods came after.' Kicker: The Veda ends its only creation account with a shrug. Every religion claims certainty about the beginning. The oldest one wrote down its doubt and kept chanting it.
notes:
Arc: Seven verses: the void, the breath without wind, desire as the first seed, the sages' cord of measurement, and the two closing verses that refuse to answer: 'he who is the overseer in highest heaven, he knows, or perhaps he does not know.'

Playbook: Argument short (F11: comments, saves). No protagonist; test against the story shorts. Famous; the hook must not be 'you think X'. Open on the line about the gods coming after.

title: 'Two sit and whisper together; the king knows it, as the third.' The Vedic god of surveillance.
angle: The Atharvaveda to a liar: the man who stands, walks, sneaks, hides, lies down, or rises, Varuna sees. Whatever two people plot, sitting together, King Varuna knows it, as the third. Kicker: Three thousand years before anyone said 'if you have nothing to hide', the Veda described a god with spies who count your blinks. It was a threat used in oaths. It still works.
notes:
Arc: The hymn to Varuna's spies: they descend from heaven, thousand-eyed; the one who flees beyond the sky is not free; the oceans are his two cups; the closing curse with Varuna's nooses on the liar.

Playbook: Argument short on truth and surveillance. The famous 'third' verse is 4.16.2 in Griffith's numbering; verify the exact verse in the packet. Pair with the published 'Atharvaveda and Varuna' explainer if any.

title: The verse used for Sati tells the widow to get up.
angle: At a Rigvedic funeral the widow lies down beside the body. Then a voice: 'Rise, come to the world of the living, woman; he is lifeless by whose side you lie.' Kicker: The Veda's funeral told the widow to stand up and live. A later misreading of one word was used to tell her to burn. The channel can show the verse; the audience can decide what one syllable is worth.
notes:
Arc: Three verses: the wives with living husbands go forward with ointment; the widow is raised and (in the text) takes the hand of the man who takes her; the bow is taken from the dead man's hand. One syllable's difference in a later reading turned 'agre' (forward) into 'agneh' (of fire).

Playbook: High F11 (argument, comments, shares) and high F6 risk (correction hook). Open on the funeral scene and the voice, not on 'you have been told'. The 'agre/agneh' claim is a scholarly argument not in the packet; present it as such or keep to the verse.

title: Viraj was a cow. Gods, men, demons, snakes and the dead each milked her, and got something different.
angle: At her birth all feared her: she will become everything. She rose; she became a cow; and everyone came with a calf and a pail. Kicker: In the Atharvaveda, poison, magic, fragrance and farming all come from one cow, depending on who did the milking. What you get from the world depends on your calf.
notes:
Arc: The gods milk her with Savitr as calf and get strength; men with Manu and get agriculture and corn; the fathers get svadha; the Asuras get maya (illusion); the snakes get poison; the Gandharvas fragrance; 'he who knows this becomes a lord of the household'.

Playbook: Allegory; argument-short material. 33 verses, repetitive; select four milkings.

title: Fire refused to lie. So a sage cursed it to eat everything.
angle: A demon asked the sacred fire: is this woman Bhrigu's wife? Fire knew that lying was a sin and that telling was a disaster. It told the truth. Kicker: Why does fire eat garbage and the holiest offering alike? Because it told the truth once and was punished for it. The Mahabharata's Agni and the Veda's Agni (who ran away from the job) are the same tired god.
notes:
Arc: The Rakshasa Puloma, once betrothed to her, claims Bhrigu's pregnant wife Puloma; Agni, asked as witness, admits she was promised to the demon first; the demon carries her off as a boar; the child Chyavana falls from the womb and burns the demon to ash; Bhrigu curses Agni: 'you shall eat everything'; Agni withdraws from all rites; the gods are starving; Brahma turns the curse: what fire touches becomes pure.

Playbook: Epic tier (Pauloma Parva, three sections). Pairs with agni-quit-fish-told (S3) as 'Agni, the god who hated his job'. Chyavana born here is the Chyavana of the published Sukanya short: a series thread.

Hindi hook draft: एक राक्षस ने अग्नि से पूछा: ये स्त्री भृगु की पत्नी है? अग्नि जानते थे, झूठ पाप है, और सच कहना तबाही। उन्होंने सच कहा।

title: He saw his ancestors hanging upside down over a pit, held by a single root a rat was chewing.
angle: The ascetic Jaratkaru had decided never to marry. On the road he saw men hanging head-down in a pit from a single grass root, and a rat gnawing it. They said: we are your ancestors. You are the root. Kicker: The whole Mahabharata is told at a sacrifice that one boy stopped, and that boy exists because his father saw a rat chewing a root. The epic's chain of causes begins with pest control.
notes:
Arc: He agrees to marry on absurd terms (a wife of his own name, given freely); the snake king Vasuki's sister Jaratkaru is offered; he leaves her the day she wakes him for the evening rite ('you insulted me'); she is already pregnant with Astika, who will stop Janamejaya's snake sacrifice.

Playbook: Epic tier (Astika Parva). The pit image is one of the best in the corpus for the house style (silhouettes, negative space). Links to the published Dog/Janamejaya short.

title: The father asked his sons for their youth. Four refused. The youngest gave it, and became king.
angle: Cursed with old age at the height of his life, Yayati went to his sons one by one: take my old age, give me your youth, for a thousand years. Kicker: The Kuru line descends from the one son who agreed to grow old for his father. The epic says the four who said no founded the peoples outside the Vedic fold. That is a strange thing for an epic to admit about ancestry.
notes:
Arc: Yadu, Turvasu, Druhyu, Anu refuse (and are cursed with the fates of their lines); Puru accepts; Yayati enjoys a thousand years, then returns it with the sentence 'desire is not quenched by enjoyment; it grows, as fire with ghee'; Puru, the youngest, is made king; the elders' descendants become outsiders.

Playbook: Epic tier (Sambhava Parva). The 'desire grows with enjoyment' verse is quotable and saved (F10). Devayani-Sharmishtha (S2) is the prequel.

title: The demons killed him three times. The third time they fed him to his own teacher.
angle: Kacha came to learn the art of raising the dead from Shukra, the demons' priest. The demons killed him, ground him, burned him, and mixed the ashes into Shukra's wine. Kicker: The only way to learn the secret was to be inside the man who knew it. The Mahabharata invented the Trojan student.
notes:
Arc: Devayani loves him and begs her father each time; Shukra revives him; the third time Kacha is inside Shukra; to come out he must learn the art and revive his teacher from within; he does; Devayani asks him to marry her; he refuses ('you are my sister now'); she curses him; he curses her back.

Playbook: Epic tier. Student/teacher thread for the Upanishad audience; a refusal of love as the turn (like the queued Urvashi). Leads into devayani-sharmishtha.

title: A student went to fetch earrings for his teacher's wife. A snake stole them on the road.
angle: Utanka's teacher's wife wanted Queen Madayanti's earrings in four days. He got them. Takshaka the snake took them from his hands while he bathed. Kicker: The snake sacrifice at which the Mahabharata is recited was started by a student with a grudge about earrings. The epic begins with petty revenge.
notes:
Arc: He follows the snake into the underworld, sees two women weaving black and white threads on a loom turned by six boys, a man on a horse (Indra and his horse); blows into the horse and fills the snake world with smoke; gets the earrings; returns on the day; then goes to Janamejaya and demands the snake sacrifice.

Playbook: Epic tier (Paushya Parva; one huge Ganguli section, 35k characters: the packet will be big, the producer may want to split by hand). Indra appears as the horseman, series link.

title: The boy raised by a deer-horned sage had never seen a woman. A kingdom needed rain.
angle: Rishyashringa, born of a doe, had seen only his father. King Lomapada's land had no rain, and the remedy was to bring the boy to the city. Kicker: The boy's innocent description of a woman, delivered to a furious father, is the funniest page in the Vana Parva. The rain, the text says, came because he left.
notes:
Arc: Courtesans arrive in a floating hermitage; the boy describes 'the student' he met to his father (the 'student' had no beard, round fruits on his chest, and sang sweetly); he is lured onto the boat; the rain comes; he marries Shanta.

Playbook: Epic tier; famous. Comedy of innocence; keep the father's reaction. The Ramayana (Dutt 1.9-1.10) gives the Dasharatha link (Shanta is Rama's sister).

title: The demon brother cooked as a goat, was eaten, and called back from inside the guest. Then he met Agastya.
angle: Ilvala would turn his brother Vatapi into a goat, feed him to a Brahmin, then call 'Vatapi, come out!' and the brother would tear through the guest's belly. Then Agastya came to dinner. Kicker: The sage who in the Rigveda negotiated with his wife for desire (the published Lopamudra) in the epic negotiates with a demon for her dowry, by digesting his brother. Same marriage, new chapter.
notes:
Arc: Agastya, seeking wealth for Lopamudra, visits kings, finds them with nothing to spare, and goes to Ilvala; eats the goat; Ilvala calls; Agastya says 'Vatapi is digested'; Ilvala pays.

Playbook: Epic tier (Vana Parva, Tirtha-yatra). Sequel to the published Lopamudra short; the audience knows the couple. Confirm 3.96-3.99 span before scripting.

title: A king wanted heaven in his body. The priests refused. So Vishvamitra built him a new one.
angle: Trishanku asked Vasishtha to send him to heaven alive. No. Vasishtha's sons cursed him into an outcaste. He went to Vishvamitra. Kicker: There is a man hanging upside down in the southern sky because two sages hated each other. The Ramayana's gods did not stop it; they made a treaty with it.
notes:
Arc: Vishvamitra performs the sacrifice; the gods do not come; by his own power he raises Trishanku bodily; Indra throws him down head-first; Vishvamitra stops him in mid-air and begins creating a second heaven with new stars and new gods; Indra negotiates: Trishanku stays, hanging, among new constellations.

Playbook: Epic tier (Bala Kanda, Dutt). Indra series crossover (Indra the negotiator). Astronomy angle. The Vasishtha-Vishvamitra feud is otherwise sparse in the corpus (BD 4.112 truncated), so this is where to tell it.

title: Indra stole the horse. Sixty thousand princes dug the earth to find it and were burned by one glance.
angle: King Sagara's horse-sacrifice needed a horse. Indra, as a Rakshasa, stole it. Sagara's sixty thousand sons dug down to the underworld to find it. Kicker: The Ganga came to earth because Indra stole a horse. The Ramayana tells the greatest river story in India as an aftermath of petty theft by the king of gods.
notes:
Arc: They dig the earth into the ocean (the 'sagara'), find the horse beside the meditating Kapila, accuse him; his glance burns them to ash; the grandson Amshuman finds the ash; Garuda tells him only the Ganga can release them; three generations later Bhagiratha brings the river down.

Playbook: Epic tier (Bala Kanda, seven sections; cut at the ash). Indra series crossover; the descent itself is another short.

title: A Brahmin's son died. The reason, said the sages, was a Shudra doing penance. Rama went to find him.
angle: A Brahmin laid his dead son at the palace gate: in your kingdom a child has died before his father. Narada said: somewhere a Shudra is practising austerities. Rama took his chariot. Kicker: The text tells it as Rama doing his duty. The audience will not agree with each other. The channel's job is to show the text exactly, and let the comments be the argument.
notes:
Arc: Rama finds Shambuka hanging head-down in penance, asks his caste and purpose (heaven, in his body), draws his sword and cuts off his head; the gods applaud; the boy revives.

Playbook: Highest controversy in the bank (F11 extreme). Only with the producer's explicit decision; if made, verbatim and without editorial. Dutt's Uttara Kanda numbering (7.87-7.88) is confirmed for 7.88; check 7.87.

title: A golden swan carried the king's love letter to the princess. Then four gods asked him to carry theirs.
angle: Nala caught a swan in his garden. It said: let me go and I will tell Damayanti about you. At her svayamvara, four gods took Nala's shape and sat beside him. Kicker: Damayanti recognised the human among four gods because he sweated, blinked and cast a shadow. The epic's definition of a man is the things gods cannot fake.
notes:
Arc: The swan courts for him; the gods (Indra, Agni, Varuna, Yama) make Nala their messenger to Damayanti against his own suit; he goes, invisible, and pleads for them; she chooses him anyway, and at the svayamvara picks the one whose garland fades, whose feet touch the ground, who blinks: the human.

Playbook: Epic tier; only the opening of the Nala story (sections 53-57) fits a short; the dice and exile are a long-form candidate (F5: long-form for subscribers). Indra appears as a suitor (series link).

title: Four brothers died drinking from a lake because they did not answer the voice. The fifth answered.
angle: 'Do not drink before you answer my questions.' Nakula drank and fell. Sahadeva, Arjuna, Bhima. Yudhishthira came last and stopped. Kicker: He could have brought back Arjuna or Bhima. He chose the brother whose mother was dead. The questions were the test; the choice was the answer.
notes:
Arc: The crane/Yaksha's questions (what is heavier than earth, faster than wind; what is the greatest wonder: that men see others die and live as if they will not); the boon: revive one brother; Yudhishthira chooses Nakula, Madri's son, so both mothers have a living son; the Yaksha is Dharma, his father.

Playbook: Epic tier; very famous; the dog short proved the audience will watch a famous Yudhishthira scene told well. Confirm the Ganguli span (Araneya Parva 3.311-3.313).
